title: "Maximum likelihood estimation"

```{r}
#| include: false
# Load ggplot2 for the consistently formatted rendered figures in this chapter.
library(ggplot2)
```

# Introduction

In this chapter, we learn how to estimate the parameters of a model by maximum likelihood
and how to calculate the uncertainty of those estimates from the likelihood. In
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd) we estimated parameters with the method of moments,
which only uses the mean and the variance of a sample. Maximum likelihood uses the
probability that the model assigns to every observation, and it applies to any model for
which we can write a probability mass or density function. This is why it is the method of
estimation in the rest of the course. The concepts of Chapter 3 (estimator, sampling
distribution, standard error and confidence interval) remain the same; we now apply them to
a different estimator.

The chapter uses two examples. The first is the sample of ten seedling counts of Chapter 3
under a Poisson model, an illustrative sample that is small enough to do the calculations
by hand and to compare every result with Chapter 3. The second is the number of calls made
by barn owl nestlings, the field data of the Chapter 3 practical (the data set `Owls` of
the package `glmmTMB`), under a Negative Binomial model with two parameters. The chapter
ends with a first tool to compare different models fitted to the same data.

# Learning goals

In this chapter, we will cover:

- the likelihood function and the log-likelihood;
- maximum likelihood estimation, analytically and by numerical optimisation;
- constraints on parameters and transformations;
- likelihood surfaces, slices and profiles for models with several parameters;
- the properties of maximum likelihood estimators in large and small samples;
- Fisher information, standard errors and Wald intervals;
- profile likelihood intervals and joint confidence regions;
- the comparison of models with the Akaike information criterion.

We will use the [Poisson](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-poisson) and
[Negative Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-negative_binomial) distributions
throughout the chapter. They are described in the
[Supplement](../Supplements/distributions.qmd).

# The likelihood function {#sec-likelihood}

The **likelihood function** is the joint probability of the observed sample, read as a
function of the parameters of the model with the data held fixed. For continuous data it is
the joint density of the sample. Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be the observations and assume that
they are i.i.d. with a distribution that has a parameter $\theta$ (as in Chapter 3,
$\theta$ stands for a parameter in general). The likelihood of $\theta$ is

$$
L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)
= P(X_1=x_1,\ldots,X_n=x_n\mid\theta)
= \prod_{i=1}^{n}P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta),
$$

where $P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta)$ is the probability mass that the model assigns to the
observation $x_i$ when the parameter is $\theta$,^[The vertical bar reads "for a given
value of": $P(X=x\mid\theta)$ is the probability of $x$ for a given value of $\theta$, and
$L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ is the likelihood of $\theta$ for a given sample. The same
symbol is used for conditional distributions, which are introduced in
[Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd).] and the symbol $\prod$ denotes a product over the
$n$ observations, in the same way as $\sum$ denotes a sum. The second equality holds
because the observations are independent, so their joint probability is the product of
their individual probabilities (see
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-joint-independence), where we announced that the
i.i.d. assumption would be fundamental for estimation). For continuous data we replace each
probability mass by the density $f_X(x_i\mid\theta)$.

This is the formula of a joint distribution from Chapter 2. What changes is what we hold
fixed. In Chapter 2 we fixed the parameters and calculated the probability of different
possible samples. Now the sample has been observed, so $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are fixed numbers,
and we look at how the probability of that sample changes as we vary $\theta$. A parameter
value under which the observed sample is more probable is better supported by the data,
which is the idea behind maximum likelihood.^[Fisher introduced the method in 1912, in a
paper that he wrote as an undergraduate student and in which he called it an "absolute
criterion". He introduced the word likelihood in 1921, to keep this quantity apart from a
probability, and the name "maximum likelihood" in 1922, in the paper that set out the
theory of the method. Choosing the parameter value under which the observations are most
probable had been anticipated in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries by Lambert,
Daniel Bernoulli and Gauss, although without a reasoned defence of the method. If you want
to read more about this history, see Aldrich (1997), "R. A. Fisher and the making of
maximum likelihood 1912–1922", *Statistical Science* 12: 162–176, and Stigler (2007), "The
epic story of maximum likelihood", *Statistical Science* 22: 598–620.] The likelihood is
the basis of everything that follows in this book: the estimates, their confidence
intervals and the comparison of models are all calculated from it.

Let's illustrate it with the ten quadrats of
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-estimates), where $X_i$ is the number of seedlings
in quadrat $i$ and $X_i \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)$. The probability mass
function of the Poisson distribution is
$P(X_i=x_i\mid\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x_i}/x_i!$. We start with a case that is small
enough to do by hand, the first three counts (3, 5 and 2). Their likelihood is the product
of three contributions:

$$
L(\lambda\mid 3,5,2)
= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{3}}{3!}\times
  \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{5}}{5!}\times
  \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{2}}{2!}
= \frac{e^{-3\lambda}\lambda^{10}}{1440}.
$$

For $\lambda=3$ this gives $e^{-9}\,3^{10}/1440\approx 0.00506$ and for $\lambda=4$ it
gives $e^{-12}\,4^{10}/1440\approx 0.00447$. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Seedling counts from the ten quadrats of Chapter 3, and the number of quadrats.
seedling_counts = c(3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 3, 4, 1, 6, 5)
n_quadrats = length(seedling_counts)

# The first three counts.
first_counts = c(3, 5, 2)

# Probability of each of the three counts at lambda = 3.
dpois(x = first_counts, lambda = 3)

# Likelihood of the three counts: prod() multiplies their probabilities.
prod(dpois(x = first_counts, lambda = 3))
prod(dpois(x = first_counts, lambda = 4))
```

The three contributions for $\lambda=3$ are approximately 0.224, 0.101 and 0.224, and
their product is the value that we calculated by hand. These three counts are slightly
more probable under a mean of 3 than under a mean of 4 (their own mean is 3.33). The
likelihood of the whole sample is calculated in the same way:

```{r}
# Likelihood of all ten counts at lambda = 3 and at lambda = 4.
prod(dpois(x = seedling_counts, lambda = 3))
prod(dpois(x = seedling_counts, lambda = 4))
```

With the ten counts the order is reversed: the likelihood is approximately
$5.2\times10^{-10}$ for $\lambda=3$ and $2.4\times10^{-9}$ for $\lambda=4$. That is, the
whole sample is about 4.5 times more probable under a mean of 4 than under a mean of 3.
Note how small both numbers are. Every observation multiplies the likelihood by a
probability smaller than one, so its value depends on the number of observations and has
no meaning by itself. What we use is the comparison between the likelihoods of different
parameter values for the same data.

A likelihood is calculated from probabilities, and it is easy to read it as the probability
of a parameter value. It is not a probability distribution for the parameter, for two
reasons.^[The likelihood is also at the core of Bayesian inference. There it is multiplied
by a prior distribution, which describes what is known about the parameter before seeing
the data, and the product is rescaled to give a probability distribution for the parameter
(the posterior distribution). [Chapter 1](../Chapter_1/Theory.qmd) explains why this book
stays with the Frequentist interpretation.] The first is conceptual. We work with
aleatoric probability ([Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd)): probabilities describe how
the data vary across replications of the experiment, while the parameter of the model is a
fixed quantity. So in the model there is nothing random about $\lambda$ to which a probability
could refer. The second is mathematical. For a fixed $\lambda$ the probabilities of all the
possible samples add up to one, but nothing forces the likelihoods of all the possible
values of $\lambda$ to do so for a fixed sample. We can check it with `integrate()`
([Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-expectations)). This function evaluates the
function that we give it at many values of $\lambda$ at once, which a likelihood written
with `prod()` cannot handle. We therefore write the Poisson likelihood of the sample as a
single expression, collecting the $n$ contributions as we did above for three counts:

$$
L(\lambda\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)
= \frac{e^{-n\lambda}\lambda^{\sum x_i}}{\prod x_i!}.
$$

In R:

```{r}
# Closed-form Poisson likelihood of a sample of counts. Unlike a product of dpois() over
# the data, this function accepts a vector of lambda values, which integrate() needs.
poisson_likelihood = function(lambda, counts) {
  exp(-length(counts) * lambda) * lambda^sum(counts) / prod(factorial(counts))
}

# Check that it gives the same likelihood as the product of probabilities.
poisson_likelihood(lambda = 4, counts = seedling_counts)

# Area under the likelihood across all possible values of lambda. The likelihood is
# tiny, so the default absolute tolerance is too coarse: we set it to zero and ask
# for a small relative error instead.
integrate(
  f = poisson_likelihood,
  lower = 0,
  upper = Inf,
  counts = seedling_counts,
  rel.tol = 1e-8,
  abs.tol = 0
)
```

The function reproduces the likelihood of the ten counts at $\lambda=4$, and the area
under the likelihood across all the values of $\lambda$ is approximately
$3.76\times10^{-9}$, which is very far from one. (The likelihood is such a small number
that `integrate()` needs stricter settings than its defaults: we ask for a small relative
error with `rel.tol` and switch off the absolute tolerance with `abs.tol = 0`.)

::: {.callout-warning title="A likelihood is not the probability of a parameter value"}
The likelihood $L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ is the probability (or density) of the
observed data for a given value of the parameter, read as a function of the parameter. It
does not add up or integrate to one over the values of the parameter, so it does not tell
us how probable a parameter value is. We use it to compare parameter values: the data are
better supported by the value with the higher likelihood.
:::

## The log-likelihood

The likelihood of ten counts is already of the order of $10^{-9}$. With a large sample the
product can become smaller than the smallest positive number that the computer can
represent, and R then returns zero. For this reason, and because sums are easier to work
with than products, we use the **log-likelihood**, the natural logarithm of the likelihood:

$$
\ell(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)
= \log L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)
= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta).
$$

The logarithm turns the product into a sum. It is an increasing function, so a parameter
value with a higher likelihood also has a higher log-likelihood, and both functions have
their maximum at the same value of $\theta$. Once the data are fixed we will write
$L(\theta)$ and $\ell(\theta)$ for short.

In R, all the `d*` functions have an argument `log`. With `log = TRUE` they return the
logarithm of the probability mass (or density), which is more accurate than calculating
the probability first and taking its logarithm afterwards. The log-likelihood is the sum
of these values:

```{r}
# Log-likelihood of the ten counts at lambda = 4: sum the log probabilities,
# using the argument log = TRUE of dpois().
sum(dpois(x = seedling_counts, lambda = 4, log = TRUE))

# The same number, from the logarithm of the product.
log(prod(dpois(x = seedling_counts, lambda = 4)))
```

Both calculations give $-19.86$ for $\lambda=4$. With ten counts the product still works.
To see when it fails, we simulate 1,000 counts from a Poisson model with $\lambda=4$:

```{r}
# Likelihood and log-likelihood of a large simulated sample of 1,000 counts at lambda = 4.
set.seed(seed = 501)
many_counts = rpois(n = 1000, lambda = 4)

# The product is smaller than the smallest positive number R can represent.
prod(dpois(x = many_counts, lambda = 4))

# The sum of log probabilities is an ordinary number.
sum(dpois(x = many_counts, lambda = 4, log = TRUE))
```

R returns zero for the product, although none of the probabilities in it is zero, whereas
the log-likelihood is an ordinary number (approximately $-2095$). From here on we always
work with log-likelihoods.

For continuous data the contributions to the likelihood are densities. Recall from
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-continuous_measurements) that a density has units
(one over the unit of the measurement), that it changes with those units and that it can
be larger than one. The log-likelihood inherits these properties: it can be positive, and
its value changes if we express the same measurements in other units. For example, if body
masses are converted from grams to kilograms, the density of every mass is multiplied by
1,000 (the same probability is spread over a thousand times fewer units), so the
log-likelihood of $n$ masses increases by $n\log(1000)$. This shift is a constant, so the
differences between the log-likelihoods of two parameter values, or of two models, are the
same in both units. In general, the value of a log-likelihood means nothing by itself, and
only differences between log-likelihoods calculated from the same data are meaningful. You
will check this with measurements of body mass in the practical.

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: crab burrows"}

Three plots on a mudflat contain 1, 0 and 2 crab burrows. Assume that the counts are i.i.d.
with a Poisson distribution. On paper, write the likelihood as a function of $\lambda$ and
calculate the likelihood and the log-likelihood for $\lambda=1$ and for $\lambda=2$ burrows
per plot. Which of the two values is better supported by the data?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The likelihood is the product of the three contributions (remember that $0!=1$):

$$
L(\lambda\mid 1,0,2)
= \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{1}}{1!}\times
  \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{0}}{0!}\times
  \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{2}}{2!}
= \frac{e^{-3\lambda}\lambda^{3}}{2}.
$$

For $\lambda=1$ the likelihood is $e^{-3}/2\approx 0.0249$ and the log-likelihood is
$-3-\log 2\approx -3.69$. For $\lambda=2$ the likelihood is $8e^{-6}/2\approx 0.0099$ and
the log-likelihood is $-6+\log 4\approx -4.61$. The data are better supported by
$\lambda=1$, which is the mean of the three counts. The difference between the two
log-likelihoods is 0.92, so the counts are about 2.5 times more probable ($e^{0.92}$)
under $\lambda=1$ than under $\lambda=2$. In R:

```{r}
# Log-likelihood of the three counts at lambda = 1 and at lambda = 2.
burrow_counts = c(1, 0, 2)
sum(dpois(x = burrow_counts, lambda = 1, log = TRUE))
sum(dpois(x = burrow_counts, lambda = 2, log = TRUE))
```

:::
::::

# Maximum likelihood estimation {#sec-maximum-likelihood}

The **maximum likelihood estimator** (MLE) of a parameter is the value of the parameter for
which the likelihood of the observed sample is highest:

$$
\hat\theta
= \underset{\theta}{\arg\max}\;L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)
= \underset{\theta}{\arg\max}\;\ell(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n),
$$

where $\arg\max$ reads "the value of $\theta$ at which the function reaches its maximum".
That is, $\max$ would give the height of the highest point and $\arg\max$ gives its
location. In plain English, the MLE is the parameter value under which the model assigns
the highest probability to the data that we observed. As with any estimator
([Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-estimates)), the rule is the estimator and the
value that it returns for our sample is the estimate; we use the abbreviation MLE for both.

In this section we find the maximum in three ways: by evaluating the log-likelihood over a
range of parameter values, with calculus, and with a numerical algorithm. The third is the
one that we use in the rest of the book, because it works for any model.

## The likelihood curve

With one parameter, the most direct way to find the maximum is to calculate the
log-likelihood for many values of the parameter and look at the result. We plot the result
as a **relative log-likelihood**, which is the difference between the log-likelihood and
its maximum,

$$
\ell(\theta)-\ell(\hat\theta),
$$

so that the curve is zero at the estimate and negative everywhere else. We draw all the
likelihood figures of this chapter on this scale, because only differences in
log-likelihood are meaningful. For the ten counts, we define a grid of values of $\lambda$
and fill a vector with the log-likelihood at each of them, using a `for` loop:

```{r}
# Candidate values of lambda (seedlings per quadrat).
lambda_grid = seq(from = 1, to = 8, by = 0.05)

# Pre-allocate a vector for the log-likelihood and fill it with a loop over the grid.
loglik_grid = rep(NA, times = length(lambda_grid))
for (i in seq_along(lambda_grid)) {
  loglik_grid[i] = sum(dpois(x = seedling_counts, lambda = lambda_grid[i], log = TRUE))
}

# which.max() returns the position of the highest value, which we use to look up the
# value of lambda with the highest log-likelihood on the grid.
lambda_grid[which.max(loglik_grid)]

# Relative log-likelihood: the difference from the highest value on the grid.
relative_loglik = loglik_grid - max(loglik_grid)

# Relative log-likelihood at 3 and at 5 seedlings per quadrat.
sum(dpois(x = seedling_counts, lambda = 3, log = TRUE)) - max(loglik_grid)
sum(dpois(x = seedling_counts, lambda = 5, log = TRUE)) - max(loglik_grid)
```

The highest log-likelihood on the grid is at 4 seedlings per quadrat
(@fig-likelihood_curve). Note that the curve is not symmetric: it falls more steeply to
the left of the maximum than to the right. The relative log-likelihood is $-1.51$ at
$\lambda=3$ and $-1.07$ at $\lambda=5$, so a mean of 5 is better supported by these data
than a mean of 3, although both are one seedling away from the estimate. We come back to
this asymmetry in @sec-likelihood-uncertainty.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-likelihood_curve
#| fig-cap: "Relative log-likelihood of the ten seedling counts under a Poisson model, as a function of the mean number of seedlings per quadrat. The vertical line marks the maximum."
# Plot the relative log-likelihood curve and mark its maximum.
curve_data = data.frame(lambda = lambda_grid, relative = relative_loglik)
ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = lambda, y = relative)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = lambda_grid[which.max(loglik_grid)],
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-8, 0)) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Mean seedlings per quadrat, ", lambda)),
    y = "Relative log-likelihood"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

A grid has two limitations: it can only return one of the values that we chose to
evaluate, and the number of combinations to evaluate grows quickly with the number of
parameters. The next two sections find the maximum without a grid.

## Analytical solution for the Poisson model

For some models the maximum can be found with calculus. At the maximum of a smooth curve
the slope is zero, so we differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter,
set the derivative to zero and solve for the parameter. For i.i.d. Poisson counts:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell(\lambda)
&= \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\left(\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x_i}}{x_i!}\right)
= -n\lambda+\log(\lambda)\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(x_i!),\\
\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda}
&= -n+\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i,\\
0 &= -n+\frac{1}{\hat\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat\lambda=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=\overline x.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last term of the log-likelihood does not contain $\lambda$, so it disappears when we
differentiate.^[The derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to a parameter is called
the **score**. The MLE is a value of the parameter at which the score is zero.] The second
derivative, $-\sum x_i/\lambda^2$, is negative, which confirms that the point where the
slope is zero is a maximum (derivatives, and what they tell us about the shape of a
function, return in [Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd)). In R:

```{r}
# The maximum likelihood estimate from the derivation is the mean of the counts.
lambda_hat = mean(seedling_counts)
lambda_hat

# The derivative of the log-likelihood, sum(x) / lambda - n, is zero at that value.
sum(seedling_counts) / lambda_hat - n_quadrats
```

So the MLE of $\lambda$ is the mean of the sample, 4 seedlings per quadrat, which is the
value that we found on the grid. It is also the method-of-moments estimator of
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-estimates). That the two methods agree is a
property of the Poisson model, and we will see in @sec-likelihood-surface that they give
different estimates for the Negative Binomial model. Also, closed-form solutions like this
one exist only for a few models.^[The Normal model is another of them. The MLE of $\mu$ is
the mean of the sample and the MLE of $\sigma^2$ is the variance with divisor $n$, that is,
the method-of-moments estimators of
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-two_parameters). The MLE of the variance is
therefore biased.] For the others, setting the derivatives to zero gives equations that
cannot be solved with algebra, and we find the maximum numerically.

## Numerical optimisation

An **optimiser** is an algorithm that searches for the parameter values at which a function
reaches its minimum. It starts from values that we provide, evaluates the function, and
moves step by step towards lower values until it cannot improve any further. In R we use
the function `optim()`. Since it minimises, we do not give it the log-likelihood but the
**negative log-likelihood** (NLL), $-\ell(\theta)$: the parameter value with the lowest NLL
is the one with the highest likelihood.

The arguments of `optim()` that we need are:

- `par`: the starting value of the parameter (a vector when there are several parameters);
- `fn`: the function to minimise, whose first argument is the parameter;
- further named arguments, which `optim()` passes on to `fn` (here `counts`, the data);
- `method`: the algorithm. We use `"BFGS"` throughout this chapter. It uses the slope of
  the function to decide in which direction to move, and
  [Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd) explains how this and other methods work.

For the Poisson model of the ten counts, starting the search at 2 seedlings per quadrat:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of Poisson counts as a function of lambda.
poisson_nll_lambda = function(lambda, counts) {
  -sum(dpois(x = counts, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE))
}

# optim() minimises fn, starting from par. Further named arguments (here counts)
# are passed on to fn.
fit_lambda = optim(
  par = 2,
  fn = poisson_nll_lambda,
  counts = seedling_counts,
  method = "BFGS"
)

# Estimate, minimum of the negative log-likelihood, and convergence code (0 = normal stop).
fit_lambda$par
fit_lambda$value
fit_lambda$convergence
```

`optim()` returns a list. Its element `par` is the value of the parameter at the minimum,
that is, the estimate: 4 seedlings per quadrat, as before. The element `value` is the NLL
at that point (19.86), so the maximum log-likelihood is $-19.86$. The element `convergence`
is a code that is zero when the algorithm stopped normally, which is the first thing to
check after every fit.

## Constraints and transformations

A **constraint** is a restriction on the values that a parameter can take. The mean
$\lambda$ of a Poisson distribution must be positive, and a probability must lie between
zero and one. An optimiser such as BFGS does not know about these restrictions. It can try
any real number, and for a negative $\lambda$ the function `dpois()` returns `NaN` (not a
number). In the fit above the search stayed among positive values, but that is not
guaranteed. In this book we deal with constraints by **transforming** the parameter: the
optimiser works with a quantity that can take any real value, and the NLL function
converts it into the parameter of the model.

For a positive parameter we use the logarithm. The optimiser searches over
$\log\lambda$, which can be any real number, and inside the function `exp()` turns it into
a positive mean:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood on the log scale: log_lambda can take any real value
# and exp() turns it into a positive mean.
poisson_nll = function(log_lambda, counts) {
  lambda = exp(log_lambda)
  -sum(dpois(x = counts, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE))
}

# Fit starting from log(2) and check the convergence code.
poisson_fit = optim(
  par = log(2),
  fn = poisson_nll,
  counts = seedling_counts,
  method = "BFGS"
)
poisson_fit$convergence

# Estimate on the log scale and transformed back to seedlings per quadrat.
poisson_fit$par
exp(poisson_fit$par)
```

The search started at $\log 2$ and ended at $\log\hat\lambda\approx 1.386$, with
convergence code 0. Transformed back with `exp()`, the estimate is again 4 seedlings per
quadrat.

For a probability $p$ the corresponding transformation is the **logit**,
$\operatorname{logit}(p)=\log\left[p/(1-p)\right]$, which covers all the real numbers as
$p$ goes from zero to one. In R, `qlogis()` calculates the logit and `plogis()` its
inverse, which turns any real number into a value between zero and one (the names come
from the logistic distribution, of which they are the quantile and cumulative probability
functions):

```{r}
# The logit transformation for a probability, and its inverse.
qlogis(p = 0.25)
plogis(q = qlogis(p = 0.25))
```

The logit of 0.25 is approximately $-1.10$, and `plogis()` returns the 0.25 that we
started with. We will use this transformation in @sec-likelihood-surface.

Fitting on a transformed scale and reporting on the original scale relies on a property of
maximum likelihood called **invariance**: the MLE of a function of a parameter is that
function of the MLE.^[See Zehna (1966), "Invariance of maximum likelihood estimators",
*Annals of Mathematical Statistics* 37: 744, for the general statement.] That is, for a
function $g$ of the parameter,

$$
\widehat{g(\theta)}=g(\hat\theta).
$$

Here the optimiser found the MLE of $\log\lambda$, and invariance tells us that its
exponential is the MLE of $\lambda$. The reason is that the transformation only relabels
the horizontal axis of the likelihood curve. Every value of $\log\lambda$ corresponds to
one value of $\lambda$ with the same likelihood, so the highest point is the same on both
scales.

Invariance also gives us the MLE of other quantities that are calculated from the
parameter. For example, under the Poisson model the probability that a quadrat has no
seedlings is $P(X=0\mid\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}$, and its MLE is $e^{-\hat\lambda}$:

```{r}
# By invariance, the estimate of the probability of an empty quadrat, exp(-lambda),
# is calculated from the estimate of lambda.
exp(-exp(poisson_fit$par))
```

That is, we estimate that approximately 1.8% of the quadrats are empty.
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-sampling_distribution) used this same quantity as
an example of a biased estimator: $\hat\lambda$ is an unbiased estimator of $\lambda$, but
$e^{-\hat\lambda}$ is a biased estimator of $e^{-\lambda}$. So invariance carries over the
estimate, but it does not carry over unbiasedness.

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: back to the ecological scale"}

A colleague fits two models with `optim()`. In the first, the parameter is the logarithm of
the mean number of ticks per lizard and the result is `par = 0.92`. In the second, the
parameter is the logit of the probability that a seed germinates and the result is
`par = -0.85`. Report both estimates on the ecological scale. Are they the maximum
likelihood estimates of the mean and of the probability?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

We apply the inverse of each transformation:

```{r}
# Inverse of the logarithm and inverse of the logit.
exp(0.92)
plogis(q = -0.85)
```

The estimates are approximately 2.5 ticks per lizard and a germination probability of
0.30. By invariance, they are the maximum likelihood estimates of the mean and of the
probability, because the optimiser found the maximum likelihood estimates of their
logarithm and logit.

:::
::::

# Models with several parameters {#sec-likelihood-surface}

With several parameters the likelihood is a function of all of them jointly, and the MLE is
the combination of values with the highest likelihood. The definitions of the previous
sections do not change, but the likelihood is now a surface over the parameters instead of
a curve. This raises questions that did not exist with one parameter: how to look at the
surface, how the estimates of the different parameters depend on each other, and how to
describe what the data say about one of them. These questions matter for the rest of the
book, because the models of Chapters 6 and 7 always have several parameters.

We will use the barn owl data of the Chapter 3 practical to illustrate these concepts. The
data set `Owls` in the package `glmmTMB` contains observations of barn owl nests (Roulin
and Bersier 2007). For each visit of a parent to a nest, the variable `SiblingNegotiation`
is the number of calls made by the nestlings. As in that practical, we keep the visits of
the female parent to nests where the nestlings had been fed (`Satiated`), so that all
counts can reasonably share one mean, and we calculate the method-of-moments estimates:

```{r}
# Load the Owls data from the glmmTMB package without attaching the package.
data(Owls, package = "glmmTMB")

# Keep the visits of the female parent to nests with satiated nestlings.
satiated_female = Owls[Owls$FoodTreatment == "Satiated" & Owls$SexParent == "Female", ]

# Number of calls at each of these visits, and the number of visits.
call_counts = satiated_female$SiblingNegotiation
n_visits = length(call_counts)

# Method-of-moments estimates, as in the practical of Chapter 3.
mu_hat = mean(call_counts)
variance_hat = mean((call_counts - mu_hat)^2)
k_mom = mu_hat^2 / (variance_hat - mu_hat)

c(n_visits = n_visits, mu_hat = mu_hat, variance_hat = variance_hat, k_mom = k_mom)
```

There are 122 visits, with a mean of 4.75 calls per visit and a variance of 42.3, almost
nine times the mean. Let $X_i$ be the number of calls at visit $i$. Because of this
overdispersion we use a
[Negative Binomial](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-negative_binomial) model with mean
$\mu$ and shape $k$,

$$
X_i \sim \operatorname{NegBin}(\mu, k), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\mu+\frac{\mu^2}{k},
$$

and we assume that the visits are i.i.d. (a simplification to which we return in
@sec-misspecified). The method of moments gives $\hat\mu=\overline x\approx 4.75$ calls
per visit and $\hat k_{\mathrm{MM}}=\hat\mu^2/(\hat\sigma^2-\hat\mu)\approx 0.60$, where
$\hat\sigma^2$ is the variance of the sample with divisor $n$ and the subscript marks the
method-of-moments estimate, as in Chapter 3.

The NLL is written as before, with two differences. `optim()` passes all the parameters to
the function as one vector, so the first argument (`par`) now holds both parameters and we
take them apart by position inside the function: `par[1]` is $\log\mu$ and `par[2]` is
$\log k$ (both parameters are positive, so we use the logarithm for both). Also, `dnbinom()`
accepts two different sets of parameters, so we name the arguments `mu` and `size`
explicitly:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood of the Negative Binomial model with mean mu and shape k.
# par holds the two parameters on the log scale: par[1] is log(mu) and par[2] is log(k).
nb_nll = function(par, counts) {
  mu = exp(par[1])
  k = exp(par[2])
  -sum(dnbinom(x = counts, mu = mu, size = k, log = TRUE))
}
```

The optimiser needs a starting value for each parameter. The method-of-moments estimates
are a sensible choice: they are quick to calculate and, being estimates of the same
parameters, they should not be far from the maximum. We give names to the elements of the
starting vector, which `optim()` keeps in its result. The argument `hessian = TRUE` asks
for the matrix of second derivatives at the minimum, which we will need in
@sec-likelihood-uncertainty:

```{r}
# Start from the method-of-moments estimates, on the log scale.
start = c(log_mu = log(mu_hat), log_k = log(k_mom))

# Fit the model; hessian = TRUE also returns the matrix of second derivatives,
# which we use later for standard errors.
owl_fit = optim(
  par = start,
  fn = nb_nll,
  counts = call_counts,
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE
)
owl_fit$convergence

# Maximum likelihood estimates on the original scale.
mu_mle = unname(exp(owl_fit$par["log_mu"]))
k_mle = unname(exp(owl_fit$par["log_k"]))
c(mu_mle = mu_mle, k_mle = k_mle)
```

The convergence code is 0. The estimate of the mean is $\hat\mu\approx 4.75$ calls per
visit, the same as with the method of moments: for a Negative Binomial model the MLE of
the mean is the mean of the sample, whatever the value of $k$. The estimate of the shape
is $\hat k\approx 0.33$.

## Comparison with the method of moments

The two methods now disagree: the estimate of the shape is 0.60 with the method of moments
and 0.33 with maximum likelihood, which implies a much larger variance. The reason is that
they use different information from the sample. The method of moments chooses the
parameters that reproduce the mean and the variance of the sample. Maximum likelihood
chooses the parameters under which the 122 observed counts are most probable, so every
count contributes with the probability that the model assigns to it. We can compare the
two pairs of estimates on those terms:

```{r}
# Log-likelihood at the maximum likelihood estimates, at the method-of-moments
# estimates, and for a Poisson model with the sample mean.
loglik_mle = -owl_fit$value
loglik_mom = -nb_nll(par = log(c(mu_hat, k_mom)), counts = call_counts)
loglik_poisson = sum(dpois(x = call_counts, lambda = mu_hat, log = TRUE))
c(mle = loglik_mle, mom = loglik_mom, poisson = loglik_poisson)

# Fraction of visits without calls: observed, and under each fitted model.
c(
  observed = mean(call_counts == 0),
  nb_mle = dnbinom(x = 0, mu = mu_mle, size = k_mle),
  nb_mom = dnbinom(x = 0, mu = mu_hat, size = k_mom),
  poisson = dpois(x = 0, lambda = mu_hat)
)

# Variance implied by the maximum likelihood fit, against the variance of the sample.
c(implied = mu_mle + mu_mle^2 / k_mle, sample = variance_hat)
```

The log-likelihood is $-299.4$ at the maximum likelihood estimates and $-306.6$ at the
method-of-moments estimates. The difference of 7.1 units means that the observed counts
are more than a thousand times more probable ($e^{7.1}\approx 1{,}200$) under the former.
The visits without calls explain why. They are 44% of the sample (54 of 122), and the
Negative Binomial distribution assigns a probability of 0.41 to a count of zero with the
maximum likelihood estimates but only 0.27 with the method-of-moments estimates
(@fig-owl_fits). The figure also shows a Poisson distribution with the same mean, under
which a visit without calls would be very rare (a probability of 0.009) and which has a
much lower log-likelihood ($-634.2$).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-owl_fits
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Relative frequencies of the number of calls per visit (bars) and probabilities under the fitted models: Negative Binomial with maximum likelihood estimates, Negative Binomial with method-of-moments estimates, and Poisson."
# Relative frequencies of each count in the sample.
count_values = 0:max(call_counts)
observed_data = data.frame(
  count = count_values,
  frequency = tabulate(call_counts + 1, nbins = length(count_values)) / n_visits
)

# Fitted probabilities for each model at every possible count.
fitted_data = rbind(
  data.frame(
    count = count_values,
    probability = dnbinom(x = count_values, mu = mu_mle, size = k_mle),
    model = "Negative Binomial (maximum likelihood)"
  ),
  data.frame(
    count = count_values,
    probability = dnbinom(x = count_values, mu = mu_hat, size = k_mom),
    model = "Negative Binomial (method of moments)"
  ),
  data.frame(
    count = count_values,
    probability = dpois(x = count_values, lambda = mu_hat),
    model = "Poisson"
  )
)

# Bars for the sample and lines with points for the models.
ggplot() +
  geom_col(
    data = observed_data,
    aes(x = count, y = frequency),
    fill = "grey90",
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = fitted_data,
    aes(x = count, y = probability, colour = model, linetype = model),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = fitted_data,
    aes(x = count, y = probability, colour = model, shape = model)
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("#D55E00", "#009E73", "grey20")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of calls per visit",
    y = "Relative frequency or probability",
    colour = NULL,
    linetype = NULL,
    shape = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "vertical")
```

The maximum likelihood fit has a price. The variance that it implies,
$\hat\mu+\hat\mu^2/\hat k\approx 74$, is much larger than the variance of the sample (42).
So neither pair of estimates reproduces every feature of the sample: the method of moments
matches the variance and misses the visits without calls, and maximum likelihood does the
opposite. This happens because the Negative Binomial model is an approximation of the data
generating process, and with an approximate model different methods of estimation settle
for different compromises. We return to this in @sec-misspecified.

<!-- AUTHOR: your view on what it means that the two estimates differ this much -->

## The likelihood surface

With two parameters we can still evaluate the log-likelihood on a grid, which now has two
dimensions: one for the values of $\mu$ and one for the values of $k$. We store the results
in a matrix with one row per value of $\mu$ and one column per value of $k$, and fill it
with two nested `for` loops:

```{r}
# Grids of candidate values for the mean (calls per visit) and the shape.
mu_grid = seq(from = 2.5, to = 9, length.out = 91)
k_grid = seq(from = 0.12, to = 0.75, length.out = 91)

# Pre-allocate a matrix and fill it with two nested loops: row i for the i-th mean
# and column j for the j-th shape.
loglik_surface = matrix(NA, nrow = length(mu_grid), ncol = length(k_grid))
for (i in seq_along(mu_grid)) {
  for (j in seq_along(k_grid)) {
    loglik_surface[i, j] = sum(
      dnbinom(x = call_counts, mu = mu_grid[i], size = k_grid[j], log = TRUE)
    )
  }
}

# Relative log-likelihood: the difference from the maximum found by optim().
relative_surface = loglik_surface - loglik_mle
```

A matrix like this one can be drawn with `contour()`, as we did in the Chapter 1 practical:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# The matrix can be drawn with contour(), as in the practical of Chapter 1.
contour(x = mu_grid, y = k_grid, z = relative_surface, levels = c(-6, -4, -3, -2, -1))
```

@fig-likelihood_surface shows the same contours. Each line joins the combinations of $\mu$
and $k$ that have the same relative log-likelihood, like the contours of the joint density
in [Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-two_continuous_variables), and the MLE is at the
top of the hill. The method-of-moments estimate lies 7.1 units below the top. The contours
are not tilted: the value of $\mu$ with the highest log-likelihood is the same for every
value of $k$ (the mean of the sample), and the best value of $k$ hardly changes with
$\mu$. The surface is not symmetric, however, as it falls more slowly towards large values
of $\mu$ and of $k$ than towards small ones.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-likelihood_surface
#| fig-cap: "Contours of the relative log-likelihood of the owl data as a function of the mean and the shape of the Negative Binomial model. The circle is the maximum likelihood estimate and the triangle is the method-of-moments estimate."
# Arrange the matrix as a data frame: mu varies fastest, as in as.vector() of the matrix.
surface_data = expand.grid(mu = mu_grid, k = k_grid)
surface_data$relative = as.vector(relative_surface)

# The two estimates, to be drawn as points.
estimate_data = data.frame(
  mu = c(mu_mle, mu_hat),
  k = c(k_mle, k_mom),
  method = c("Maximum likelihood", "Method of moments")
)

# Contours of the relative log-likelihood with both estimates.
ggplot() +
  geom_contour(
    data = surface_data,
    aes(x = mu, y = k, z = relative),
    breaks = c(-12, -9, -6, -4, -3, -2, -1),
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = estimate_data,
    aes(x = mu, y = k, shape = method),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Mean number of calls per visit, ", mu)),
    y = expression(paste("Shape, ", italic(k))),
    shape = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Parameterisation and the shape of the surface

The same model can be written with different sets of parameters, each of which is called a
**parameterisation**. For the Negative Binomial distribution, R's own parameters are the
shape $k$ (`size`) and a probability $p$ (`prob`), which is related to the mean through
$p=k/(k+\mu)$ (the "Inverse" line of the
[supplement entry](../Supplements/distributions.qmd#sec-negative_binomial)). Let's fit the
same model to the same data in these parameters, with $\log k$ and $\operatorname{logit}p$
as the transformed parameters:

```{r}
# Negative log-likelihood in R's own parameters: shape k (size) and probability p (prob).
# par[1] is log(k) and par[2] is logit(p).
nb_prob_nll = function(par, counts) {
  k = exp(par[1])
  p = plogis(par[2])
  -sum(dnbinom(x = counts, size = k, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}

# Starting values: the method-of-moments shape and p = k / (k + mu).
start_prob = c(log_k = log(k_mom), logit_p = qlogis(k_mom / (k_mom + mu_hat)))

owl_fit_prob = optim(
  par = start_prob,
  fn = nb_prob_nll,
  counts = call_counts,
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE
)
owl_fit_prob$convergence

# Estimates on the original scale and the maximum log-likelihood.
k_mle_prob = unname(exp(owl_fit_prob$par["log_k"]))
p_mle = unname(plogis(owl_fit_prob$par["logit_p"]))
c(k_mle_prob = k_mle_prob, p_mle = p_mle, loglik = -owl_fit_prob$value)

# By invariance, p equals k / (k + mu) evaluated at the first fit.
k_mle / (k_mle + mu_mle)
```

The maximum log-likelihood is $-299.44$, the same as before, and so is
$\hat k\approx 0.33$. The estimate of the probability is $\hat p\approx 0.064$, which is
the value of $\hat k/(\hat k+\hat\mu)$ from the first fit, as invariance says (the two
numbers differ in the fifth decimal because each search stops when it is close enough to
the maximum). It is the same model at the same maximum. What changes is the shape of the surface around the maximum, which we
calculate on a grid as before:

```{r}
# Grids of candidate values for the shape and the probability.
k_grid_prob = seq(from = 0.12, to = 0.75, length.out = 91)
p_grid = seq(from = 0.02, to = 0.16, length.out = 91)

# Fill the matrix of log-likelihoods with two nested loops.
loglik_surface_prob = matrix(NA, nrow = length(k_grid_prob), ncol = length(p_grid))
for (i in seq_along(k_grid_prob)) {
  for (j in seq_along(p_grid)) {
    loglik_surface_prob[i, j] = sum(
      dnbinom(x = call_counts, size = k_grid_prob[i], prob = p_grid[j], log = TRUE)
    )
  }
}
relative_surface_prob = loglik_surface_prob - loglik_mle
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-surface_size_prob
#| fig-cap: "Contours of the relative log-likelihood of the owl data as a function of the shape k and the probability p of the Negative Binomial model. The circle is the maximum likelihood estimate."
# Arrange the matrix as a data frame: k varies fastest.
surface_prob_data = expand.grid(k = k_grid_prob, p = p_grid)
surface_prob_data$relative = as.vector(relative_surface_prob)

# Contours with the maximum likelihood estimate.
ggplot() +
  geom_contour(
    data = surface_prob_data,
    aes(x = k, y = p, z = relative),
    breaks = c(-12, -9, -6, -4, -3, -2, -1),
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(k = k_mle_prob, p = p_mle),
    aes(x = k, y = p),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Shape, ", italic(k))),
    y = expression(paste("Probability, ", italic(p)))
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

In @fig-surface_size_prob the contours are tilted: a larger $k$ goes with a larger $p$. In
these parameters the mean of the distribution is $k(1-p)/p$, and the data determine the
mean number of calls well. So a higher value of $k$ can be compensated by a higher value of
$p$ that keeps the mean close to 4.75, with little loss of likelihood. We saw tilted
contours in the joint density of the diameter and height of a tree in
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-two_continuous_variables), where they described two
variables that change together. Here they describe two parameters whose estimates depend on
each other, which has consequences for slices and profiles (below) and for the uncertainty
of the estimates (@sec-likelihood-uncertainty).

This book writes distributions in terms of their mean where possible, because we normally
model the effect of covariates on the mean (see the
[Supplement](../Supplements/distributions.qmd)). For the Negative Binomial distribution
that parameterisation also gives estimates that hardly depend on each other, as
@fig-likelihood_surface showed. The choice of parameters also matters for numerical
optimisation, which is a topic of [Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd).

## Slices and profiles

A surface can only be drawn for two parameters, and even then we usually want to know what
the data say about one parameter at a time. There are two ways of reducing a likelihood
surface to a curve for one parameter, and they answer different questions.

A **likelihood slice** fixes the other parameters at one value, normally their estimates,
and varies the parameter of interest. For the shape $k$ in the parameters $k$ and $p$, the
slice is $\ell(k,\hat p)$, a cut through the surface along a straight line.

A **profile likelihood** re-estimates the other parameters for every value of the parameter
of interest:

$$
\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(k)=\max_{p}\,\ell(k,p).
$$

That is, for each value of $k$ we find the value of $p$ that maximises the log-likelihood
with $k$ held fixed, and we record that maximum. The parameters that are re-estimated are
called **nuisance parameters**: they are needed to define the model, but they are not the
parameter that the question is about. Which parameter is of interest and which is a
nuisance depends on the question, and we will profile each parameter in turn.

To calculate both curves we loop over a grid of values of $k$. The slice evaluates the
log-likelihood with $p$ fixed at $\hat p$. The profile needs an optimisation inside the
loop, with an NLL in which $k$ is given and only $\operatorname{logit}p$ is searched. Each
of these inner searches starts at the joint estimate:

```{r}
# Fine grid of shape values on which the slice and the profile are evaluated.
k_fine = seq(from = 0.12, to = 0.75, length.out = 127)

# Negative log-likelihood as a function of logit(p) only, for a given shape k.
nll_given_k = function(logit_p, k, counts) {
  -sum(dnbinom(x = counts, size = k, prob = plogis(logit_p), log = TRUE))
}

# Slice: p is fixed at its estimate. Profile: for each k, p is re-estimated with optim(),
# starting from the joint estimate.
slice_loglik = rep(NA, times = length(k_fine))
profile_loglik = rep(NA, times = length(k_fine))
profile_p = rep(NA, times = length(k_fine))
profile_convergence = rep(NA, times = length(k_fine))
for (i in seq_along(k_fine)) {
  slice_loglik[i] = sum(
    dnbinom(x = call_counts, size = k_fine[i], prob = p_mle, log = TRUE)
  )
  inner_fit = optim(
    par = owl_fit_prob$par["logit_p"],
    fn = nll_given_k,
    k = k_fine[i],
    counts = call_counts,
    method = "BFGS"
  )
  profile_loglik[i] = -inner_fit$value
  profile_p[i] = plogis(inner_fit$par)
  profile_convergence[i] = inner_fit$convergence
}

# Relative log-likelihoods and the range of k within 1.92 of the maximum
# (the cutoff is explained in the section on profile likelihood intervals).
slice_relative = slice_loglik - loglik_mle
profile_relative = profile_loglik - loglik_mle
range(k_fine[slice_relative >= -1.92])
range(k_fine[profile_relative >= -1.92])

# All inner fits stopped normally.
all(profile_convergence == 0)
```

All the inner fits converged. The last lines give the range of values of $k$ for which
each curve is within 1.92 units of its maximum, a cutoff that we justify in
@sec-profile_intervals: 0.26 to 0.41 for the slice and 0.24 to 0.45 for the profile.

```{r}
#| include: false
# In the parameters mu and k, the best mu for any k is the sample mean, so the
# profile of k equals the slice at the estimate of mu. Check this on the same grid.
slice_k_mu = rep(NA, times = length(k_fine))
profile_k_mu = rep(NA, times = length(k_fine))
for (i in seq_along(k_fine)) {
  slice_k_mu[i] = sum(
    dnbinom(x = call_counts, mu = mu_mle, size = k_fine[i], log = TRUE)
  )
  inner_fit = optim(
    par = log(mu_mle),
    fn = function(log_mu, k, counts) {
      -sum(dnbinom(x = counts, mu = exp(log_mu), size = k, log = TRUE))
    },
    k = k_fine[i],
    counts = call_counts,
    method = "BFGS"
  )
  profile_k_mu[i] = -inner_fit$value
}
max(abs(slice_k_mu - profile_k_mu))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-slice_profile
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Slice and profile of the log-likelihood for the shape k of the Negative Binomial model fitted to the owl data. Left: contours in k and p with the slice (dashed line) and the values of p that maximise the log-likelihood for each k (solid line). Right: relative log-likelihood along the slice and along the profile; the horizontal line is at -1.92."
library(patchwork)

# Left panel: contours with the slice and the path of the profile.
path_data = data.frame(k = k_fine, p = profile_p)
left_panel = ggplot() +
  geom_contour(
    data = surface_prob_data,
    aes(x = k, y = p, z = relative),
    breaks = c(-12, -9, -6, -4, -3, -2, -1),
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = p_mle, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#D55E00") +
  geom_line(data = path_data, aes(x = k, y = p), colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(k = k_mle_prob, p = p_mle),
    aes(x = k, y = p),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Shape, ", italic(k))), y = expression(paste("Probability, ", italic(p)))) +
  theme_classic()

# Right panel: relative log-likelihood along the slice and along the profile.
curve_data = rbind(
  data.frame(k = k_fine, relative = slice_relative, curve = "Slice"),
  data.frame(k = k_fine, relative = profile_relative, curve = "Profile")
)
right_panel = ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = k, y = relative, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -1.92, colour = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-6, 0)) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Shape, ", italic(k))), y = "Relative log-likelihood", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

left_panel | right_panel
```

@fig-slice_profile shows why the two curves differ. In the left panel, the slice follows
the horizontal line at $\hat p$, which leaves the high part of the surface quickly because
the contours are tilted. The profile follows the ridge of the surface: for each $k$ it
moves to the best $p$. Both pass through the MLE, and everywhere else the profile is
higher than the slice, since it is the maximum over all the values of $p$ (right panel).
The slice is therefore narrower. It describes what the data would say about $k$ if we
knew that $p$ is exactly 0.064, whereas the profile takes into account that $p$ is
estimated from the same data.

How much the two curves differ depends on the parameterisation. With the mean as the
second parameter, the slice and the profile of $k$ coincide, because the best $\mu$ is the
mean of the sample for every value of $k$. The profile itself does not depend on how the
nuisance parameter is written: maximising over $p$ or over $\mu$ gives the same curve for
$k$. A slice does depend on it.

We will use profiles to calculate confidence intervals (@sec-profile_intervals). Slices
need no optimisation, so they are a quick way to inspect a fitted model, and they return
as a diagnostic in [Chapter 8](../Chapter_8/Theory.qmd).

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: slice or profile"}

A colleague fits a Weibull model, which has a shape and a scale, to the lifespans of
leaves. To describe what the data say about the shape, she calculates the log-likelihood
for a range of values of the shape, with the scale fixed at its estimate. Is this a slice
or a profile? What would she have to change to obtain the other curve? Which of the two
takes the uncertainty about the scale into account?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

It is a slice, because the scale stays at one value. For a profile she would re-estimate
the scale with `optim()` for every value of the shape and record the highest
log-likelihood. The profile takes the uncertainty about the scale into account. The slice
treats the scale as known, so it is narrower than the profile unless the estimates of the
two parameters do not depend on each other.

:::
::::

::: {.callout-note title="Explore a likelihood surface"}
Kristoffer Magnusson's
[interactive page on maximum likelihood](https://rpsychologist.com/likelihood/) lets you
do by hand what an optimiser does. It uses a Normal model with two parameters, a mean and a
variance, and a sample of ten observations. In the part "Likelihood Calculation", move the
sliders of the mean and the variance and watch how the contribution of each observation
and the log-likelihood change. In "Finding the Maximum Likelihood Estimates", follow how an
algorithm climbs the log-likelihood step by step. The last part of the page is about
hypothesis tests, which we do not use in this course.
:::

# Properties of maximum likelihood estimators {#sec-mle_properties}

An MLE is an estimator, so everything that we learnt in
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-sampling_distribution) applies to it: it has a
sampling distribution across hypothetical experiments, a bias, a variance and a standard
error. In a finite sample we do not know that sampling distribution in general. For large
samples, however, there are results that hold for the MLEs of a very wide class of
models,^[These results require some conditions on the model, known as regularity
conditions. In words: the parameter is not on the boundary of its range (e.g., a variance
of exactly zero), the support of the distribution does not depend on the parameter, the
log-likelihood is a smooth function of the parameters, and the number of parameters does
not grow with the sample size.] and they are the reason why this book uses maximum
likelihood. This section presents three of them (consistency, asymptotic normality and
efficiency) and then looks at what happens in small samples and when the model is not a
good description of the data generating process.

We check each result with the same simulation. As in the Chapter 3 practical, we simulate
hypothetical experiments from a model whose parameters we know: a Negative Binomial model
with the maximum likelihood estimates for the owls as parameters ($\mu=4.75$ and
$k=0.327$). We simulate 2,000 hypothetical experiments for each of three sample sizes: 20,
122 (the size of the owl sample) and 500 visits. For each experiment we calculate the
maximum likelihood estimate of $k$ with `optim()`, as above, and the method-of-moments
estimate. We study $k$ because the MLE of $\mu$ is the mean of the sample, whose behaviour
we already know from Chapter 3. The code of the simulation is not shown (you will write a
simulation of this kind in the practical). It stores the estimates in two matrices,
`sim_k_ml` and `sim_k_mom`, with one row per hypothetical experiment and one column per
sample size.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
# Fit the Negative Binomial model to a sample of counts by maximum likelihood.
# Returns the estimates, the method-of-moments shape, and whether the fit converged.
# The starting values are the method-of-moments estimates when they exist.
fit_negbin = function(counts, hessian = FALSE) {
  mu_start = mean(counts)
  variance_start = mean((counts - mu_start)^2)
  k_start_mom = ifelse(
    variance_start > mu_start,
    mu_start^2 / (variance_start - mu_start),
    NA
  )
  fit = optim(
    par = log(c(mu_start, ifelse(is.na(k_start_mom), 1, k_start_mom))),
    fn = nb_nll,
    counts = counts,
    method = "BFGS",
    hessian = hessian
  )
  list(
    mu = exp(fit$par[1]),
    k = exp(fit$par[2]),
    k_mom = k_start_mom,
    loglik = -fit$value,
    convergence = fit$convergence,
    hessian = fit$hessian
  )
}

# Hypothetical experiments from a Negative Binomial model whose parameters are the
# maximum likelihood estimates for the owls, for three numbers of visits.
set.seed(seed = 601)
n_experiments = 2000
visit_sizes = c(20, 122, 500)
sim_k_ml = matrix(NA, nrow = n_experiments, ncol = length(visit_sizes))
sim_k_mom = matrix(NA, nrow = n_experiments, ncol = length(visit_sizes))
sim_converged = matrix(NA, nrow = n_experiments, ncol = length(visit_sizes))
for (s in seq_along(visit_sizes)) {
  for (e in seq_len(n_experiments)) {
    counts = rnbinom(n = visit_sizes[s], mu = mu_mle, size = k_mle)
    fit = fit_negbin(counts = counts)
    sim_k_ml[e, s] = fit$k
    sim_k_mom[e, s] = fit$k_mom
    sim_converged[e, s] = fit$convergence == 0
  }
}
```

## Consistency

In [Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-large_samples) we defined a consistent estimator
as one that converges in probability to the parameter as the sample size grows. Maximum
likelihood estimators are **consistent** when the observations are i.i.d. from the
model.^[The consistency of maximum likelihood estimators was proved rigorously, under
regularity conditions, by Abraham Wald (1949) and by others in the 1930s and 1940s.] For
the shape of the Negative Binomial model, with $\hat k_n$ the MLE calculated from $n$
visits and any positive margin $\varepsilon$:

$$
\lim_{n \to \infty}
P\left(\left|\hat k_n - k\right| \ge \varepsilon\right)=0.
$$

In plain English, the chance that the estimate misses $k$ by $\varepsilon$ or more becomes
small as we observe more visits. In the simulation we can calculate this chance for a
margin of 0.1:

```{r}
# Fraction of the estimates that differ by 0.1 or more from the shape used to simulate,
# for 20, 122 and 500 visits. colMeans() calculates the mean of each column, and the
# mean of TRUE and FALSE values is the fraction of TRUE values.
colMeans(abs(sim_k_ml - k_mle) >= 0.1)
```

With 20 visits, 46% of the estimates differ from the $k$ used to simulate by 0.1 or more.
With 122 visits it is 7%, and with 500 visits none of the 2,000 estimates does.

Why should the maximum of the likelihood be close to the parameter in a large sample?
Chapter 3 gives us an intuition. If we divide the log-likelihood by $n$, which does not
move its maximum, we obtain

$$
\frac{1}{n}\ell(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log P(X_i=x_i\mid\theta),
$$

the mean of $\log P(X=x\mid\theta)$ over the sample. This is an expectation under the
empirical distribution of the sample
([Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-samples)). As the sample grows, the empirical
distribution converges to the distribution that generated the data (the Glivenko–Cantelli
theorem), so the function that we maximise converges to the expectation of
$\log P(X=x\mid\theta)$ under that distribution. It can be shown that this expectation is
highest when $\theta$ is the parameter that generated the data (we will see why in
@sec-misspecified).

## Asymptotic normality and Fisher information

[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-large_samples) ended with the central limit
theorem: the mean of $n$ i.i.d. observations is asymptotically normal. It also announced
that this chapter would generalise the result to other parameters. The generalisation is
that the MLE of any parameter is **asymptotically normal**: as the sample grows, its
sampling distribution approaches a Normal distribution centred on the
parameter.^[Fisher used the large-sample standard error of maximum likelihood estimators
in 1922 and developed the concept of information in 1925, with arguments that were not
rigorous. The result was made rigorous by Wald (1943) and by Cramér (1946), whose
treatment states the conditions explicitly.] For one parameter:

$$
\hat\theta \overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Normal}\left(\theta,\frac{1}{\mathcal I(\theta)}\right)
\quad\text{for sufficiently large }n,
$$

where $\mathcal I(\theta)$ is the **Fisher information** that the sample contains about
$\theta$. In plain English, across hypothetical experiments with a large sample the
estimates fall around the parameter in the shape of a bell, and the more information the
sample contains, the narrower the bell.

The information measures how sharply the log-likelihood is curved around its maximum. We
calculate it from our sample as the **observed information**, which is minus the second
derivative of the log-likelihood at the estimate,^[Strictly, the Fisher information in the
result above is the **expected information**: the expectation of $-\ell''(\theta)$ across
hypothetical experiments. The observed information is calculated from the log-likelihood of
the sample that we have, and the two agree in large samples. Efron and Hinkley (1978)
compared them and argued for the observed information.] and from it we obtain an estimate
of the variance and of the standard error of the estimator:

$$
\hat{\mathcal I}=-\ell''(\hat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta)=\frac{1}{\hat{\mathcal I}},
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathcal I}}}.
$$

The second derivative measures how fast the slope of a curve changes. At a maximum it is
negative, and the more negative it is, the faster the log-likelihood falls as we move away
from the estimate. A sharply curved log-likelihood therefore means that the data
discriminate well among parameter values, which corresponds to a small variance of the
estimator. A flat log-likelihood means that many parameter values are almost equally well
supported, which corresponds to a large variance.

For the Poisson model we can do the calculation by hand. Differentiating the
log-likelihood a second time gives $\ell''(\lambda)=-\sum x_i/\lambda^2$. At
$\hat\lambda=\overline x$ the sum of the counts is $n\hat\lambda$, so

$$
\hat{\mathcal I}=\frac{n\hat\lambda}{\hat\lambda^2}=\frac{n}{\hat\lambda}=\frac{10}{4}=2.5,
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\lambda)=\frac{\hat\lambda}{n}=0.4,
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\lambda)=\sqrt{0.4}\approx 0.63.
$$

This is exactly the plug-in standard error that we calculated in
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-standard_errors) from the formula for the variance
of a mean. Maximum likelihood gives it to us from the curvature of the log-likelihood,
which we can calculate for any model, also when there is no formula for the variance of
the estimator. We can verify our math with R:

```{r}
# Observed information of the Poisson model at the estimate: -l''(lambda_hat) = sum(x) / lambda_hat^2,
# which equals n / lambda_hat at lambda_hat = mean(x).
observed_information = sum(seedling_counts) / lambda_hat^2
observed_information

# Approximate variance of the estimator and its standard error (seedlings per quadrat).
approximate_variance = 1 / observed_information
standard_error = sqrt(approximate_variance)
c(approximate_variance = approximate_variance, standard_error = standard_error)

# The plug-in standard error of Chapter 3.
sqrt(lambda_hat / n_quadrats)
```

With several parameters, the information is a matrix that contains the second derivatives
of the log-likelihood with respect to every pair of parameters. The matrix of second
derivatives of a function is called its **Hessian**. With `hessian = TRUE`, `optim()`
returns the Hessian of the function that it minimised, the NLL, at the estimates. This is
the observed information matrix, and its inverse approximates the variances of the
estimates and the covariances between them. We use it in @sec-likelihood-uncertainty.

::: {.callout-note title="Asymptotic normality of maximum likelihood estimators"}
For a large sample of i.i.d. observations from the model, the sampling distribution of a
maximum likelihood estimator is approximately Normal, centred on the parameter, with a
variance equal to the inverse of the Fisher information. The observed information (minus
the second derivative of the log-likelihood at the estimate) estimates it from the sample.
:::

How large the sample needs to be depends on the model and on the parameter, so we look at
the simulation (@fig-sampling_distribution_k). With 20 visits the estimates of $k$ are
strongly skewed. Half of them are below 0.36, but a long tail to the right reaches values
above 1, and their mean is 0.40, against the 0.327 used to simulate. A Normal curve with
the same mean and standard deviation is a poor description of this distribution. With 500
visits the estimates have a mean of 0.329, their distribution is nearly symmetric and the
Normal curve is close to it.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-sampling_distribution_k
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Maximum likelihood estimates of the shape k from 2,000 hypothetical experiments with 20 and with 500 visits, simulated from a Negative Binomial model with the estimates for the owls as parameters. The vertical line is the shape used in the simulation and the curves are Normal distributions with the mean and standard deviation of the estimates."
library(patchwork)

# Histogram of the estimates for one number of visits, with its Normal approximation.
plot_sampling_k = function(column, bin_width) {
  estimates = sim_k_ml[, column]
  estimate_grid = seq(from = min(estimates), to = max(estimates), length.out = 200)
  approximation = data.frame(
    estimate = estimate_grid,
    density = dnorm(x = estimate_grid, mean = mean(estimates), sd = sd(estimates))
  )
  ggplot(data.frame(estimate = estimates), aes(x = estimate)) +
    geom_histogram(
      aes(y = after_stat(density)),
      binwidth = bin_width,
      fill = "grey90",
      colour = "grey40"
    ) +
    geom_line(
      data = approximation,
      aes(x = estimate, y = density),
      colour = "#D55E00",
      linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = k_mle, linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(
      title = paste(visit_sizes[column], "visits"),
      x = expression(paste("Estimated shape, ", italic(k))),
      y = "Density"
    ) +
    theme_classic()
}

plot_sampling_k(column = 1, bin_width = 0.04) |
  plot_sampling_k(column = 3, bin_width = 0.01)
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: information in a sample"}

Bird territories are counted along 25 transects of the same length, and the total is 64
territories. Under a Poisson model, calculate the MLE of the mean number of territories per
transect, the observed information and the standard error. What would the observed
information and the standard error be with 100 transects and the same mean count?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The MLE is the mean of the sample, $\hat\lambda=64/25=2.56$ territories per transect. The
observed information is $n/\hat\lambda=25/2.56\approx 9.8$ and the standard error is
$1/\sqrt{9.8}\approx 0.32$ territories per transect, which is the same as
$\sqrt{\hat\lambda/n}$. With 100 transects the information would be four times larger
($100/2.56\approx 39.1$) and the standard error half as large (0.16): the information adds
up over the observations.

:::
::::

## Efficiency

The mean squared error (MSE) of
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-sampling_distribution) allows us to compare
estimators of the same parameter. In large samples, where the bias is negligible, this
comes down to comparing their variances. How small can the variance of an estimator be?
The **Cramér–Rao bound** states that no unbiased estimator has a variance smaller than the
inverse of the Fisher information:^[The bound was derived independently in the 1940s by
Fréchet, Darmois, Rao and Cramér, and it carries the names of the last two. Fisher had
already obtained a version for large samples in 1925. The word "regular" in the statement
of efficiency excludes estimators that are constructed to beat the bound at particular
values of the parameter, such as the one proposed by Hodges in 1951.]

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\theta)\ge\frac{1}{\mathcal I(\theta)}
\quad\text{for any unbiased estimator }\tilde\theta.
$$

In plain English, the information in a sample sets a limit to the precision with which a
parameter can be estimated from it, whatever the method. The inverse of the information is
also the variance that an MLE approaches as the sample grows (previous section). So an MLE
is **asymptotically efficient**: in large samples no other regular estimator is more
precise.

This is the answer to the question of why we do not continue with the method of moments,
which is easier to calculate. Both estimators of $k$ are consistent, but they are not
equally precise. We compare them with the estimates stored in the simulation:

```{r}
# The method of moments gives no estimate of k when the variance of a sample is not
# larger than its mean. Count the samples in which that happened.
sum(is.na(sim_k_mom))

# Mean, standard deviation and mean squared error of both estimators of k for each
# number of visits. Column s of sim_k_ml and sim_k_mom holds the 2,000 estimates for
# the s-th number of visits.
efficiency_table = data.frame(
  visits = visit_sizes,
  mean_ml = NA, sd_ml = NA, mse_ml = NA,
  mean_mom = NA, sd_mom = NA, mse_mom = NA
)
for (s in seq_along(visit_sizes)) {
  ml = sim_k_ml[, s]
  mom = sim_k_mom[, s]
  efficiency_table$mean_ml[s] = mean(ml)
  efficiency_table$sd_ml[s] = sd(ml)
  efficiency_table$mse_ml[s] = mean((ml - k_mle)^2)
  efficiency_table$mean_mom[s] = mean(mom)
  efficiency_table$sd_mom[s] = sd(mom)
  efficiency_table$mse_mom[s] = mean((mom - k_mle)^2)
}

# Show the table with three significant digits.
signif(efficiency_table, digits = 3)
```

The method of moments returned an estimate in all the 6,000 samples. In the table, the
columns ending in `ml` describe the maximum likelihood estimates and those ending in `mom`
the method-of-moments estimates. With 122 visits the standard deviation of the estimates is
0.055 for maximum likelihood against 0.086 for the method of moments, and the MSE is 0.0031
against 0.0085. The difference does not disappear in a larger sample, as the theory
predicts: with 500 visits the standard deviations are 0.024 and 0.042. Standard errors
decrease with the square root of the sample size, so the method of moments would need
about $(0.086/0.055)^2\approx 2.5$ times as many visits to estimate $k$ with the precision
that maximum likelihood achieves with 122. With 20 visits maximum likelihood also has the
smaller MSE (0.042 against 0.112).

## Bias in finite samples

Asymptotic normality tells us that the sampling distribution of an MLE is centred on the
parameter in a large sample. In a small sample this need not be the case, and the table
above already suggests it: the mean of the estimates of $k$ from 20 visits is 0.40. The
bias relative to the $k$ used to simulate is:

```{r}
# Relative bias of the maximum likelihood estimator of k for each number of visits.
data.frame(
  visits = efficiency_table$visits,
  relative_bias = efficiency_table$mean_ml / k_mle - 1
)
```

With 20 visits, $\hat k$ is on average 21% larger than the $k$ used to simulate. With 122
visits the bias is 2.7% and with 500 visits 0.6%. This is the general behaviour: MLEs are
in general biased in finite samples, and the bias decreases as the sample grows.^[Corrections
of the bias exist for particular models. Dividing by $n-1$ in the estimator of a variance
is one of them ([Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-two_parameters)). Restricted
maximum likelihood (REML) is the general approach to reduce the bias of the estimates of
variance parameters, and it is used with the models for grouped observations of
[Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd).] It decreases faster than the standard error, so in
a large sample it is negligible compared with the variation of the estimates across
hypothetical experiments. The warning about finite samples in
[Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-large_samples) applies to maximum likelihood as
much as to the method of moments: for a small sample the properties of this section are
approximations, and simulation is the way to check them.

## Misspecified models {#sec-misspecified}

All the properties above assume that the observations are a random sample from the model.
[Chapter 1](../Chapter_1/Theory.qmd) described the model as an approximation of the data
generating process, so this assumption is never exactly right. A model is **misspecified**
when it does not contain the distribution of the data generating process, whatever the
values of its parameters. What does the MLE estimate in that case?

The answer is that, as the sample grows, the MLE converges to the parameter values for
which the model distribution is closest to the distribution of the data generating
process.^[Kullback and Leibler (1951) introduced this measure of "information for
discrimination" between two distributions, which is now called the Kullback–Leibler
divergence. Maximum likelihood estimation under a misspecified model is studied by White
(1982), "Maximum likelihood estimation of misspecified models", *Econometrica*; Huber
(1967) is an earlier treatment.] Closeness is measured by the **Kullback–Leibler
divergence**, which for a discrete variable is

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta)
= E_g\left[\log\frac{g(X)}{P(X\mid\theta)}\right]
= \sum_x g(x)\log\frac{g(x)}{P(X=x\mid\theta)},
$$

where $g(x)$ is the probability with which the data generating process produces the value
$x$, $P(X=x\mid\theta)$ is the probability that the model assigns to it, and $E_g$ is an
expectation ([Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-expectations)) calculated with the
probabilities $g$. In plain English, the divergence is the average, over the values that
the data generating process produces, of the logarithm of the ratio between the
probability of a value and the probability that the model gives to it. It is zero when the
model assigns the right probability to every value, and positive otherwise.

This completes the intuition that we gave for consistency. The expectation of
$\log P(X\mid\theta)$, which the log-likelihood divided by $n$ approaches in a large
sample, is the only part of the divergence that depends on $\theta$, and it enters with a
minus sign. Maximising the likelihood therefore amounts to minimising the divergence
between the model and the data generating process. When the model contains the
distribution that generated the data, the minimum is zero and it is reached at the
parameter that generated them, which is consistency. When it does not, the MLE settles on
the best approximation that the model can offer.

For the owls there are two signs that the Negative Binomial model with i.i.d. visits is an
approximation. The first is the comparison in @sec-likelihood-surface: the model fitted by
maximum likelihood reproduces the visits without calls better than the variance of the
counts (74 against 42 in the sample). The second is the design of the study. The 122
visits come from a limited number of nests:

```{r}
# The visits come from a limited number of nests.
length(unique(satiated_female$Nest))
```

There are 24 nests, and visits to the same nest are likely to resemble each other, so the
visits are not independent. The Chapter 3 practical already described the i.i.d. assumption
as a simplification for these data, and the models for observations nested in groups are
the subject of [Chapter 7](../Chapter_7/Theory.qmd). The estimates that we obtained are
still the best that this model can do for these data. The standard errors and confidence
intervals of the next section are calculated as if the model had generated the data, so
with a misspecified model they are approximations too.

<!-- AUTHOR: your view on what a wrong model means in practice -->

# Uncertainty from the likelihood {#sec-likelihood-uncertainty}

A confidence interval for a parameter can be calculated from a likelihood in two ways. The
**Wald interval** uses the asymptotic normality of the MLE and the curvature of the
log-likelihood at its maximum, which gives the standard error. The **profile likelihood
interval** uses the whole shape of the log-likelihood around the maximum. In this book the
profile likelihood interval is the reference method, and the Wald interval is the fast
approximation that software usually reports. This section explains both, shows when they
differ and checks their coverage by simulation.

<!-- AUTHOR: why you prefer profile intervals -->

## Standard errors and Wald intervals

In [Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-confidence_intervals) we defined the Wald
interval^[The interval is named after Abraham Wald, who developed in 1943 the large-sample
test on which it is based.] as
$\hat\theta\pm z_{0.975}\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)$ and justified it with
the approximate normality of the estimator. For an MLE the standard error comes from the
observed information (@sec-mle_properties). For the Poisson model we calculated it by
hand, $\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\lambda)=\sqrt{\hat\lambda/n}\approx 0.63$, so the
interval is the one of Chapter 3:

```{r}
# Wald interval for the Poisson mean, on the original scale (as in Chapter 3).
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
wald_original = lambda_hat + c(-1, 1) * critical_value * sqrt(lambda_hat / n_quadrats)
wald_original
```

That is, 2.76 to 5.24 seedlings per quadrat.

With `optim()` we do not need to derive the second derivative by hand, because the Hessian
contains it. However, `optim()` calculates the Hessian of the function that it minimised
with respect to the parameter that it searched over, which in our fit is $\log\lambda$. So
the standard error that we obtain from it is the standard error of the estimate of
$\log\lambda$:

```{r}
# Refit the Poisson model on the log scale, now with the Hessian.
poisson_fit = optim(
  par = log(2),
  fn = poisson_nll,
  counts = seedling_counts,
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE
)

# The Hessian is a 1 by 1 matrix; take its single element. Its inverse is the
# approximate variance of the estimate of log(lambda).
hessian_log = poisson_fit$hessian[1, 1]
se_log_lambda = sqrt(1 / hessian_log)
c(hessian_log = hessian_log, se_log_lambda = se_log_lambda)
```
