```{r}
# Wald interval on the log scale, back-transformed to seedlings per quadrat.
wald_log = exp(poisson_fit$par + c(-1, 1) * critical_value * se_log_lambda)
wald_log
```

A fit with one parameter returns a matrix with one row and one column, from which we take
the single element. The Hessian is 40 (you can check that the second derivative of the NLL
with respect to $\log\lambda$ is $n\lambda$) and the standard error of the estimate of
$\log\lambda$ is $1/\sqrt{40}\approx 0.158$. We calculate the Wald interval on the log
scale, where this standard error applies, and transform its endpoints back with `exp()`:
2.93 to 5.45 seedlings per quadrat.

This interval differs from the first one, although both are 95% Wald intervals for the
same parameter and the same data. A Wald interval depends on the scale on which it is
calculated, because the Normal approximation is applied to a different quantity in each
case ($\hat\lambda$ or its logarithm). The interval from the log scale is not symmetric
around the estimate and it cannot include negative values, which Chapter 3 noted as a
defect of the Wald interval on the original scale. Note that we transformed the endpoints
of the interval and not the standard error: a standard error on the log scale cannot be
converted into seedlings per quadrat with `exp()`. That conversion requires the delta
method, which we introduce in [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd).

The Wald interval amounts to replacing the log-likelihood by a parabola with the same
curvature at the maximum,

$$
\ell(\theta)-\ell(\hat\theta)\approx
-\frac{(\theta-\hat\theta)^2}{2\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)^2},
$$

which is why it is also called a quadratic approximation, and the interval a quadratic
interval. The approximation is good when the log-likelihood is close to a parabola on the
scale that we use, and we saw in @fig-likelihood_curve that for the ten counts it is not
symmetric.

With two parameters the Hessian is a matrix with two rows and two columns, and we need its
inverse. In R, `solve()` applied to a matrix returns its inverse (matrices were introduced
in the Chapter 1 practical), `diag()` extracts the diagonal of a matrix, which here holds
the variances of the two estimates, and `sqrt()` turns them into standard errors. For the
owl fit:

```{r}
# Two parameters: solve() returns the inverse of the Hessian, which approximates the
# covariance matrix of the estimates of log(mu) and log(k). diag() takes its diagonal
# (the variances) and sqrt() gives the standard errors.
owl_covariance = solve(owl_fit$hessian)
owl_se = sqrt(diag(owl_covariance))
owl_se

# Wald intervals on the log scales, back-transformed to the original scales.
owl_wald_lower = exp(owl_fit$par - critical_value * owl_se)
owl_wald_upper = exp(owl_fit$par + critical_value * owl_se)
owl_wald = rbind(
  mu = c(estimate = mu_mle, lower = owl_wald_lower[[1]], upper = owl_wald_upper[[1]]),
  k = c(estimate = k_mle, lower = owl_wald_lower[[2]], upper = owl_wald_upper[[2]])
)
owl_wald

# Standard deviation of the estimates of log(k) across the hypothetical experiments
# with 122 visits simulated earlier (second column of sim_k_ml).
sd(log(sim_k_ml[, 2]))
```

The standard errors are 0.164 for the estimate of $\log\mu$ and 0.165 for the estimate of
$\log k$, and the back-transformed Wald intervals are 3.45 to 6.55 calls per visit for
$\mu$ and 0.24 to 0.45 for $k$. The simulation of @sec-mle_properties used the sample size
and the estimates of this fit, so we can compare the standard error with it: the standard
deviation of the estimates of $\log k$ across the 2,000 hypothetical experiments with 122
visits is 0.161, close to the 0.165 that we obtained from the Hessian of a single sample.

It is instructive to compare the interval for $\mu$ with the one of the Chapter 3
practical, which went from 3.60 to 5.91 calls per visit. The estimate of the mean is the
same, but its uncertainty is now larger. To see why, we calculate the standard error of
the mean in calls per visit with the formula of that practical,
$\sqrt{(\hat\mu+\hat\mu^2/\hat k)/n}$, once with the maximum likelihood estimate of $k$ and
once with the method-of-moments estimate:

```{r}
# Standard error of the mean (calls per visit) with the maximum likelihood estimate of k
# and with the method-of-moments estimate used in Chapter 3.
se_mu_nb = sqrt((mu_mle + mu_mle^2 / k_mle) / n_visits)
se_mu_mom = sqrt((mu_hat + mu_hat^2 / k_mom) / n_visits)
c(se_mu_nb = se_mu_nb, se_mu_mom = se_mu_mom)

# Wald interval for mu on the original scale, with the first of these standard errors.
mu_mle + c(-1, 1) * critical_value * se_mu_nb
```

The standard error is 0.78 calls per visit with the maximum likelihood estimate of $k$,
against 0.59 in Chapter 3, because the Negative Binomial model fitted by maximum
likelihood has a larger variance than the sample. With this standard error, a Wald
interval on the original scale goes from 3.23 to 6.28 calls per visit. So an interval
depends on the model, on the method of estimation and, for a Wald interval, on the scale.

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: an interval from the log scale"}

In the practice about ticks on lizards, the fit on the log scale returned `par = 0.92`.
The sample had 20 lizards and the Hessian returned by `optim()` is 50.2. Calculate a 95%
Wald interval for the mean number of ticks per lizard. Why is it not symmetric around the
estimate?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The standard error of the estimate of the logarithm of the mean is
$1/\sqrt{50.2}\approx 0.141$. We calculate the interval on the log scale and transform its
endpoints:

```{r}
# Wald interval on the log scale, back-transformed to ticks per lizard.
se_log_mean = sqrt(1 / 50.2)
exp(0.92 + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(p = 0.975) * se_log_mean)
```

The interval goes from approximately 1.9 to 3.3 ticks per lizard, around an estimate of
2.5. It is symmetric on the log scale, and `exp()` stretches the part above the estimate
more than the part below it.

:::
::::

## Covariance between estimates

The inverse of the Hessian contains more than variances. Its off-diagonal elements are the
**covariances** between the estimates, which describe how the estimates of two parameters
vary together across hypothetical experiments. A covariance divided by the two standard
errors is the correlation between the estimates
([Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-two_continuous_variables) introduced the
correlation as a parameter of the bivariate Normal distribution), and `cov2cor()` does this
conversion for a whole matrix:

```{r}
# Correlations between the estimates, from the inverse Hessian.
cov2cor(owl_covariance)

# The same for the parameters k and p, whose estimates are correlated.
cov2cor(solve(owl_fit_prob$hessian))
```

For the estimates of $\log\mu$ and $\log k$ the correlation is zero to four decimals. For
those of $\log k$ and $\operatorname{logit}p$ it is 0.71: hypothetical experiments that
overestimate $k$ would also tend to overestimate $p$. This is the tilt of
@fig-surface_size_prob expressed as a number. In large samples the estimates of two
parameters jointly follow a bivariate Normal distribution, and the contours of its density
have the shape of the contours of the likelihood near the maximum.

Correlated estimates are the rule in the models of the following chapters. In particular,
the parameters of a response curve are usually strongly correlated
([Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd)).

## Profile likelihood intervals {#sec-profile_intervals}

The second type of interval does not rely on the curvature at one point. It is based on
**Wilks' theorem**,^[Wilks (1938). The theorem is about the ratio between two maximised
likelihoods (a difference between two log-likelihoods is the logarithm of a likelihood
ratio), and it holds under the regularity conditions of @sec-mle_properties. The profile
likelihood interval follows from it.] which describes how far below its maximum the
log-likelihood is at the parameter value that generated the data. Let $\theta_0$ be that
value for the parameter of interest. Then

$$
2\left[\ell(\hat\theta)-\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta_0)\right]
\overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}\chi^2_1
\quad\text{for sufficiently large }n,
$$

where $\ell(\hat\theta)$ is the maximum of the log-likelihood,
$\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta_0)$ is the profile log-likelihood at $\theta_0$ (with a single
parameter it is the log-likelihood itself) and $\chi^2_1$ is the chi-squared distribution
with one degree of freedom, which is the distribution of the square of a standard Normal
variable. In plain English, across hypothetical experiments the parameter value that
generated the data is rarely far down the slope of the profile: twice its distance to the
top behaves like the square of a standard Normal variable.^[The same result is the basis
of the likelihood ratio test, which compares two nested models by calculating a p-value
from the chi-squared distribution. As with p-values in general, we do not use it in this
course.] In R, the quantiles of this distribution are calculated with `qchisq()`:

```{r}
# Cutoff for the relative profile log-likelihood: half the 95% quantile of a
# chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom.
qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 1)
sqrt(qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 1))
cutoff = qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 1) / 2
cutoff
```

The 0.95 quantile is 3.84, which is the square of the 1.96 of the Wald interval. So in
about 95% of hypothetical experiments the profile log-likelihood at $\theta_0$ is within
$3.84/2=1.92$ units of the maximum. The **profile likelihood interval** contains all the
values of the parameter whose relative profile log-likelihood is above $-1.92$. It
contains $\theta_0$ in exactly those experiments, which gives it a coverage of
approximately 95%. This is the cutoff that we used in @sec-likelihood-surface to compare
the slice and the profile.

::: {.callout-note title="Profile likelihood interval"}
An approximate 95% confidence interval for a parameter contains all the values whose
profile log-likelihood is within 1.92 units of the maximum log-likelihood (half the 0.95
quantile of a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom). The other parameters
of the model are re-estimated for each value.
:::

The Poisson model has one parameter, so the profile is the log-likelihood itself, and the
endpoints of the interval are the two values of $\lambda$ at which the relative
log-likelihood equals $-1.92$ (@fig-likelihood_curve). To find them we use `uniroot()`,
which searches for the value at which a function crosses zero. Its main arguments are the
function (`f`) and an `interval` in which to search, whose two ends must give values of
opposite sign. We give it the relative log-likelihood plus the cutoff, which is zero at
the endpoints of the confidence interval, positive at the estimate (where it equals 1.92)
and negative far from it. There is one crossing on each side of the estimate, so we call
`uniroot()` twice: between 0.5 and $\hat\lambda$, and between $\hat\lambda$ and 20. At
those two outer values the log-likelihood is far below the cutoff (@fig-likelihood_curve
shows this for the range from 1 to 8).

```{r}
# Relative log-likelihood of the Poisson model: with one parameter it is also the profile.
poisson_relative_loglik = function(lambda, counts) {
  sum(dpois(x = counts, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE)) -
    sum(dpois(x = counts, lambda = mean(counts), log = TRUE))
}

# uniroot() finds where a function crosses zero inside an interval whose ends give
# values of opposite sign. We look for the two values of lambda where the relative
# log-likelihood equals -cutoff, one below the estimate and one above it.
lambda_lower = uniroot(
  f = function(lambda) poisson_relative_loglik(lambda, counts = seedling_counts) + cutoff,
  interval = c(0.5, lambda_hat),
  tol = 1e-8
)$root
lambda_upper = uniroot(
  f = function(lambda) poisson_relative_loglik(lambda, counts = seedling_counts) + cutoff,
  interval = c(lambda_hat, 20),
  tol = 1e-8
)$root
likelihood_interval = c(lambda_lower, lambda_upper)
likelihood_interval

# The three intervals for lambda (seedlings per quadrat).
poisson_intervals = rbind(
  "Wald, original scale" = wald_original,
  "Wald, log scale" = wald_log,
  "Likelihood" = likelihood_interval
)
colnames(poisson_intervals) = c("lower", "upper")
poisson_intervals
```

The element `root` of the result is the crossing point, and the argument `tol` sets the
precision with which it is located. The likelihood interval goes from 2.89 to 5.37
seedlings per quadrat. The matrix at the end of the output collects the three intervals
that we have calculated for $\lambda$. The likelihood interval is not symmetric: it
extends 1.11 below the estimate and 1.37 above it, following the asymmetry of the curve.
It also does not depend on the scale, because a value of $\lambda$ and its logarithm have
the same likelihood, so we would obtain the same interval by searching over
$\log\lambda$. The Wald interval from the log scale is closer to it than the Wald interval
on the original scale.

For the owls we need the profile of each parameter. We write a function that returns the
relative profile log-likelihood for a given value of $\mu$. Inside it, `optim()`
re-estimates $\log k$ with $\mu$ held fixed, starting from the joint estimate. A second
pair of functions does the same for $k$:

```{r}
# Profile log-likelihood of mu relative to the maximum: for each mu the shape is
# re-estimated with optim() on log(k), starting from the joint estimate.
nll_given_mu = function(log_k, mu, counts) {
  -sum(dnbinom(x = counts, mu = mu, size = exp(log_k), log = TRUE))
}
profile_relative_mu = function(mu, counts) {
  inner_fit = optim(
    par = owl_fit$par["log_k"],
    fn = nll_given_mu,
    mu = mu,
    counts = counts,
    method = "BFGS"
  )
  -inner_fit$value - loglik_mle
}

# The same for k, re-estimating the mean on the log scale.
nll_given_k_mu = function(log_mu, k, counts) {
  -sum(dnbinom(x = counts, mu = exp(log_mu), size = k, log = TRUE))
}
profile_relative_k = function(k, counts) {
  inner_fit = optim(
    par = owl_fit$par["log_mu"],
    fn = nll_given_k_mu,
    k = k,
    counts = counts,
    method = "BFGS"
  )
  -inner_fit$value - loglik_mle
}

# Both profiles are zero at the joint estimate.
c(profile_relative_mu(mu = mu_mle, counts = call_counts),
  profile_relative_k(k = k_mle, counts = call_counts))
```

Both profiles are zero at the joint estimates (up to the precision of the optimiser), as
they should be. We find the endpoints with `uniroot()` as before. For $\mu$ we search
between 1 and the estimate and between the estimate and 20, and for $k$ between 0.05 and
the estimate and between the estimate and 2, which are values far outside the region of
high likelihood in @fig-likelihood_surface:

```{r}
# Endpoints of the profile likelihood interval of mu, below and above the estimate.
mu_lower = uniroot(
  f = function(mu) profile_relative_mu(mu, counts = call_counts) + cutoff,
  interval = c(1, mu_mle),
  tol = 1e-8
)$root
mu_upper = uniroot(
  f = function(mu) profile_relative_mu(mu, counts = call_counts) + cutoff,
  interval = c(mu_mle, 20),
  tol = 1e-8
)$root

# Endpoints of the profile likelihood interval of k.
k_lower = uniroot(
  f = function(k) profile_relative_k(k, counts = call_counts) + cutoff,
  interval = c(0.05, k_mle),
  tol = 1e-8
)$root
k_upper = uniroot(
  f = function(k) profile_relative_k(k, counts = call_counts) + cutoff,
  interval = c(k_mle, 2),
  tol = 1e-8
)$root

# Profile intervals next to the Wald intervals calculated on the log scales.
owl_intervals = rbind(
  "mu, profile" = c(mu_lower, mu_upper),
  "mu, Wald" = owl_wald["mu", c("lower", "upper")],
  "k, profile" = c(k_lower, k_upper),
  "k, Wald" = owl_wald["k", c("lower", "upper")]
)
colnames(owl_intervals) = c("lower", "upper")
owl_intervals
```

The profile likelihood intervals are 3.49 to 6.68 calls per visit for $\mu$ and 0.24 to
0.45 for $k$. For $k$ the Wald interval from the log scale is almost the same (0.237 to
0.453 against 0.235 to 0.451). For $\mu$ the profile likelihood interval reaches further
above the estimate than the Wald interval from the log scale (6.68 against 6.55), and
much further than the Wald interval on the original scale (3.23 to 6.28).
@fig-profile_interval shows the reason. The parabola in the figure is the quadratic
approximation on the original scale, drawn with the standard error of 0.78 calls per
visit. To the right of the estimate the profile falls more slowly than the parabola, and
to the left it falls faster.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-profile_interval
#| fig-cap: "Relative profile log-likelihood of the mean number of calls per visit for the owl data (solid line) and the quadratic approximation that corresponds to the Wald interval on the original scale (dashed line). The horizontal line is the cutoff of the 95% interval, at -1.92, and the vertical lines mark the endpoints of the profile likelihood interval."
# Evaluate the profile on a grid of means.
mu_fine = seq(from = 2.5, to = 9, length.out = 131)
profile_mu_values = rep(NA, times = length(mu_fine))
for (i in seq_along(mu_fine)) {
  profile_mu_values[i] = profile_relative_mu(mu = mu_fine[i], counts = call_counts)
}

# Quadratic approximation around the estimate, with the standard error of mu from the
# Negative Binomial variance (se_mu_nb).
quadratic_values = -(mu_fine - mu_mle)^2 / (2 * se_mu_nb^2)

curve_data = rbind(
  data.frame(mu = mu_fine, relative = profile_mu_values, curve = "Profile"),
  data.frame(mu = mu_fine, relative = quadratic_values, curve = "Quadratic approximation")
)
ggplot(curve_data, aes(x = mu, y = relative, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -cutoff, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(mu_lower, mu_upper), colour = "grey40", linetype = "dotted") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-6, 0)) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Mean number of calls per visit, ", mu)),
    y = "Relative log-likelihood",
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: nest success"}

Of 40 monitored nests, 26 fledged at least one chick, so the MLE of the probability of
success under a Binomial model is $\hat p=0.65$. The relative log-likelihood for several
values of $p$ is:

| $p$ | 0.45 | 0.50 | 0.55 | 0.60 | 0.65 | 0.70 | 0.75 | 0.80 | 0.85 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Relative log-likelihood | $-3.23$ | $-1.83$ | $-0.83$ | $-0.21$ | $0$ | $-0.23$ | $-0.99$ | $-2.44$ | $-4.89$ |

Which of these values are inside the 95% likelihood interval? Between which values of the
table do the endpoints of the interval lie? Is the interval symmetric around the estimate?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The interval contains the values with a relative log-likelihood above $-1.92$, that is,
those from 0.50 to 0.75. The lower endpoint lies between 0.45 and 0.50, close to 0.50
(where the curve is at $-1.83$), and the upper endpoint between 0.75 and 0.80. The
interval is not symmetric: the curve falls faster above the estimate than below it. With
`uniroot()` the endpoints are 0.496 and 0.785:

```{r}
# Relative log-likelihood of the Binomial model plus the cutoff, as a function of p.
nest_function = function(p) {
  dbinom(x = 26, size = 40, prob = p, log = TRUE) -
    dbinom(x = 26, size = 40, prob = 0.65, log = TRUE) +
    qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 1) / 2
}

# One crossing below the estimate and one above it.
uniroot(f = nest_function, interval = c(0.2, 0.65), tol = 1e-8)$root
uniroot(f = nest_function, interval = c(0.65, 0.95), tol = 1e-8)$root
```

:::
::::

## Joint confidence regions

Wilks' theorem also applies to several parameters at once. If we fix two parameters at the
values that generated the data, twice the drop in log-likelihood from the maximum follows
approximately a chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom (the distribution of
the sum of the squares of two independent standard Normal variables):

```{r}
# Cutoff for a joint region of two parameters: half the 95% quantile of a
# chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom.
qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2)
joint_cutoff = qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2) / 2
joint_cutoff
```

The 0.95 quantile is 5.99, so the cutoff is 3.00 units of log-likelihood instead of 1.92.
The combinations of $\mu$ and $k$ whose relative log-likelihood is above $-3.00$ form an
approximate 95% **joint confidence region** for the two parameters. It is the area inside
one contour of the likelihood surface (@fig-joint_region).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-joint_region
#| fig-cap: "Approximate joint 95% confidence region for the mean and the shape of the Negative Binomial model fitted to the owl data (contour in vermillion). The segments along the axes are the 95% profile likelihood intervals of each parameter."
# Contours of the surface, the contour of the joint region, the estimate and the
# profile intervals of the two parameters drawn along the axes.
ggplot() +
  geom_contour(
    data = surface_data,
    aes(x = mu, y = k, z = relative),
    breaks = c(-12, -9, -6, -4, -2, -1),
    colour = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_contour(
    data = surface_data,
    aes(x = mu, y = k, z = relative),
    breaks = -joint_cutoff,
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = data.frame(mu = mu_mle, k = k_mle),
    aes(x = mu, y = k),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 3
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = mu_lower, xend = mu_upper, y = min(k_grid), yend = min(k_grid),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = min(mu_grid), xend = min(mu_grid), y = k_lower, yend = k_upper,
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Mean number of calls per visit, ", mu)),
    y = expression(paste("Shape, ", italic(k)))
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

The region extends beyond the profile likelihood interval of each parameter, because it
answers a different question. A profile likelihood interval is a statement about one
parameter, whatever the value of the other: it is the range that the contour at $-1.92$
covers along one axis. The joint region is a statement about both parameters at once: in
about 95% of hypothetical experiments it contains the pair of values that generated the
data. Capturing two parameters simultaneously is more demanding than capturing one, so the
cutoff is further from the maximum. For the same reason, the rectangle formed by the two
separate intervals is not a 95% region for the pair. We use an interval when a question is
about one parameter and a region when it is about a combination of parameters.

## Coverage checked by simulation

As in [Chapter 3](../Chapter_3/Theory.qmd#sec-confidence_intervals), we check the coverage
of the intervals with a simulation in which we know the parameters. For each hypothetical
experiment we calculate both types of interval and record whether each of them contains
the parameter used to simulate. For the likelihood intervals we do not need to search for
the endpoints: the interval contains a value exactly when the relative profile
log-likelihood at that value is above $-1.92$. We consider four cases (@fig-coverage).

The first two cases use a Poisson model and compare the Wald interval on the original
scale with the likelihood interval, with 5,000 hypothetical experiments each. Chapter 3
warned that the Wald interval does badly when the expected total count $n\lambda$ is
small, so the first case has $\lambda=0.5$ and 10 quadrats, an expected total of five
seedlings. The coverage of the Wald interval is 0.871, far from the intended 0.95, and
that of the likelihood interval is 0.931. (A sample in which all the quadrats are empty
gives an estimate of zero, for which neither interval can be calculated. We count it as a
miss for both; it happens in less than 1% of these experiments.) The second case is the
one of Chapter 3, with $\lambda=4$ and 30 quadrats, where both intervals are on target
(0.952 and 0.954).

The other two cases use the Negative Binomial model with the owl estimates as parameters
and compare, for the shape $k$, the Wald interval calculated on the log scale with the
profile likelihood interval, with 2,000 hypothetical experiments each. With 20 visits the
coverages are 0.946 and 0.942, and with 122 visits they are 0.959 and 0.960. Here the two
intervals perform equally well. A coverage simulated with 2,000 experiments has itself a
standard error of about 0.005 ($\sqrt{0.95\times 0.05/2000}$), so differences of this size
are within the noise of the simulation.

```{r}
#| include: false
# Cutoff of the relative log-likelihood for 95% profile intervals (one parameter).
cutoff = qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 1) / 2
critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)

# Poisson model: coverage of the Wald interval on the original scale and of the
# likelihood interval, for a mean lambda and a number of quadrats.
poisson_coverage = function(lambda, n_quadrats, n_experiments) {
  # One row per hypothetical experiment, one column per quadrat.
  counts = matrix(
    rpois(n = n_experiments * n_quadrats, lambda = lambda),
    nrow = n_experiments,
    ncol = n_quadrats
  )
  totals = rowSums(counts)
  estimates = totals / n_quadrats

  # Wald interval on the original scale.
  se = sqrt(estimates / n_quadrats)
  wald_covered = estimates - critical_value * se <= lambda &
    lambda <= estimates + critical_value * se

  # The likelihood interval contains lambda when its relative log-likelihood is within
  # the cutoff. A sample of zeros has no finite estimate of the interval: a miss.
  relative = -n_quadrats * (lambda - estimates) + totals * log(lambda / estimates)
  likelihood_covered = totals > 0 & relative >= -cutoff

  c(wald = mean(wald_covered), likelihood = mean(likelihood_covered))
}

set.seed(seed = 701)
coverage_poisson_small = poisson_coverage(lambda = 0.5, n_quadrats = 10, n_experiments = 5000)
coverage_poisson_large = poisson_coverage(lambda = 4, n_quadrats = 30, n_experiments = 5000)

# Negative Binomial model (owl estimates): coverage of the Wald interval for k on the log
# scale and of the profile interval. The profile at the generating k is the log-likelihood
# with mu set to the sample mean, which is its maximum for any k.
negbin_coverage = function(n_visits, n_experiments) {
  wald_covered = rep(NA, times = n_experiments)
  profile_covered = rep(NA, times = n_experiments)
  for (e in seq_len(n_experiments)) {
    counts = rnbinom(n = n_visits, mu = mu_mle, size = k_mle)
    fit = fit_negbin(counts = counts, hessian = TRUE)
    se_log_k = tryCatch(sqrt(solve(fit$hessian)[2, 2]), error = function(e) NA)
    if (fit$convergence == 0 && !is.na(se_log_k)) {
      wald_covered[e] = abs(log(k_mle) - log(fit$k)) <= critical_value * se_log_k
      profile_loglik_k0 = sum(
        dnbinom(x = counts, mu = mean(counts), size = k_mle, log = TRUE)
      )
      profile_covered[e] = profile_loglik_k0 - fit$loglik >= -cutoff
    }
  }
  c(
    wald = mean(wald_covered, na.rm = TRUE),
    profile = mean(profile_covered, na.rm = TRUE),
    failed = sum(is.na(wald_covered))
  )
}

set.seed(seed = 702)
coverage_nb_small = negbin_coverage(n_visits = 20, n_experiments = 2000)
coverage_nb_large = negbin_coverage(n_visits = 122, n_experiments = 2000)

# Collect the results for the figure.
coverage_results = data.frame(
  case = rep(
    c(
      "Poisson, λ = 0.5,\n10 quadrats",
      "Poisson, λ = 4,\n30 quadrats",
      "Negative Binomial, k,\n20 visits",
      "Negative Binomial, k,\n122 visits"
    ),
    each = 2
  ),
  interval = rep(c("Wald", "Likelihood"), times = 4),
  coverage = c(
    coverage_poisson_small[["wald"]], coverage_poisson_small[["likelihood"]],
    coverage_poisson_large[["wald"]], coverage_poisson_large[["likelihood"]],
    coverage_nb_small[["wald"]], coverage_nb_small[["profile"]],
    coverage_nb_large[["wald"]], coverage_nb_large[["profile"]]
  )
)
coverage_results$case = factor(coverage_results$case, levels = unique(coverage_results$case))
coverage_results
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-coverage
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Simulated coverage of nominal 95% Wald and likelihood intervals. Poisson cases: 5,000 hypothetical experiments, interval for the mean on the original scale. Negative Binomial cases: 2,000 hypothetical experiments, interval for the shape k, with the Wald interval calculated on the log scale. The dashed line is the nominal level."
# Coverage by case and type of interval; the dashed line is the intended 0.95.
ggplot(coverage_results, aes(x = case, y = coverage, shape = interval, linetype = interval)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.4),
    colour = "#D55E00",
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.8, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Simulated coverage", shape = NULL) +
  guides(linetype = "none") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

So the profile likelihood interval was as good as the Wald interval or better in every
case, and clearly better where the log-likelihood is far from a parabola. A Wald interval
calculated on a suitable scale, such as the logarithm of a positive parameter, can be just
as good, and it needs one fit instead of many. In the practical you will run a simulation
of this kind for another model.

# Model comparison with AIC {#sec-aic}

More than one model can be plausible for the same data.
[Chapter 2](../Chapter_2/Theory.qmd#sec-discrete_distributions) gave heuristics to choose
a distribution and announced formal tools, and the likelihood provides the first of them.
We have compared parameter values of one model through their log-likelihoods, so it is
natural to compare two models through their maximum log-likelihoods. That comparison is
not fair when the models have different numbers of parameters. A model with more
parameters has more freedom to adapt to the particular sample that we collected, including
its accidental features. When one model contains the other as a special case (the Negative
Binomial distribution approaches the Poisson distribution as $k$ grows), its maximum
log-likelihood can never be lower.

The **Akaike information criterion** (AIC) corrects the maximum log-likelihood for the
number of parameters:

$$
\mathrm{AIC}=2K-2\,\ell(\hat\theta),
$$

where $\ell(\hat\theta)$ is the maximum log-likelihood of the model and $K$ is the number
of parameters that were estimated (we write $K$ because $k$ is the shape of the Negative
Binomial distribution). The log-likelihood enters with a minus sign, so among models
fitted to the same data the one with the lowest AIC is preferred. Like the value of a
log-likelihood, the AIC of one model means nothing by itself: only differences between
models fitted to the same observations, in the same units, are meaningful.

The criterion follows from the ideas of @sec-misspecified. Apart from a constant that is
the same for all the models, AIC estimates how far the fitted model is from the data
generating process in terms of the Kullback–Leibler divergence, when the fitted model is
used to predict new data from the same process.^[Akaike (1973, 1974) derived the criterion
as an estimate of a loss based on the Kullback–Leibler divergence. Reading the term $2K$
as a correction for using the same data twice is the usual interpretation of the
criterion.] The maximum log-likelihood alone is too optimistic for that purpose, because
the same data were used to fit the model and to evaluate it, and the term $2K$ corrects
for this. In plain English, AIC rewards a model for assigning a high probability to the
data and penalises it for each parameter that it needed to do so.

For the owls we have fitted two models: the Poisson model, with one parameter, and the
Negative Binomial model, with two.

```{r}
# Maximised log-likelihood, number of estimated parameters K and AIC for the two models
# fitted to the owl data. AIC = 2K - 2 * log-likelihood.
aic_table = data.frame(
  model = c("Poisson", "Negative Binomial"),
  K = c(1, 2),
  loglik = c(loglik_poisson, loglik_mle)
)
aic_table$aic = 2 * aic_table$K - 2 * aic_table$loglik

# Only differences in AIC matter: difference from the lowest value.
aic_table$delta_aic = aic_table$aic - min(aic_table$aic)
aic_table
```

The AIC is 1270.3 for the Poisson model and 602.9 for the Negative Binomial model. The
difference of 667 units in favour of the Negative Binomial model is very large compared
with the two units that its additional parameter costs, in agreement with what
@fig-owl_fits showed.

AIC ranks the candidate models that we give it. It does not tell us whether the best of
them describes the data well: the Negative Binomial model is far better than the Poisson
model for the owls, and we have seen that it is still an approximation.
[Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd) returns to model comparison with further tools (the
Bayesian information criterion and cross-validation) and with checks of goodness of fit.

<!-- AUTHOR: your take on AIC and how you use differences in practice -->

:::: {.callout-important title="Practice: waiting for a pollinator"}

The waiting times between visits of pollinators to a flower are fitted with an Exponential
model, which has one parameter, and with a Gamma model, which has two. The maximum
log-likelihoods are $-231.0$ and $-230.4$. Calculate the AIC of both models. Which one has
the lower AIC? Could the log-likelihood of the Gamma model have been the lower of the two?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

For the Exponential model $\mathrm{AIC}=2\times 1+2\times 231.0=464.0$ and for the Gamma
model $\mathrm{AIC}=2\times 2+2\times 230.4=464.8$. The Exponential model has the lower
AIC, although its log-likelihood is lower: the improvement of 0.6 units of log-likelihood
does not compensate for the additional parameter. A difference of 0.8 units of AIC is very
small, so these data hardly distinguish the two models. The log-likelihood of the Gamma
model could not have been the lower one, because the Exponential distribution is a Gamma
distribution with a shape of one, and a model that contains another as a special case fits
the same data at least as well.

:::
::::

# Summary

The likelihood is the joint probability (or density) of the observed sample, read as a
function of the parameters with the data held fixed. For i.i.d. observations it is a
product of contributions, and its logarithm, the log-likelihood, is a sum. The maximum
likelihood estimate is the parameter value with the highest likelihood. For a few models
it can be derived with calculus, and in general we find it by minimising the negative
log-likelihood with `optim()`. Constraints on parameters are handled with transformations
(the logarithm for positive parameters and the logit for probabilities), and invariance
allows us to transform the estimates back.

With several parameters the likelihood is a surface. Its shape depends on the
parameterisation, although the maximum and the fitted model do not. A slice fixes the
other parameters, whereas a profile re-estimates them for every value of the parameter of
interest, so the profile takes their uncertainty into account.

Maximum likelihood estimators are consistent, asymptotically normal and asymptotically
efficient: in large samples they are centred on the parameter and no other regular
estimator is more precise. Their variance is the inverse of the Fisher information, which
we calculate from the curvature of the log-likelihood at its maximum. In finite samples
they are in general biased, and their sampling distribution can be far from Normal. When
the model is misspecified, the estimator converges to the parameter values that bring the
model closest to the data generating process, as measured by the Kullback–Leibler
divergence.

Uncertainty is calculated from the same likelihood. The inverse of the Hessian returned by
`optim()` gives standard errors and covariances on the scale that was optimised, and Wald
intervals are calculated on that scale and transformed back. Profile likelihood intervals
contain the values whose profile log-likelihood is within 1.92 units of the maximum; they
do not depend on the scale and they follow the asymmetry of the likelihood. A joint
confidence region for two parameters uses a cutoff of 3.00. Simulation shows how close the
coverage of each interval is to the confidence level. Finally, AIC compares models fitted
to the same data by penalising the maximum log-likelihood for the number of parameters.

So far every observation had the same distribution. In
[Chapter 5](../Chapter_5/Theory.qmd) we study deterministic functions that describe how an
expected response changes with a predictor, and in [Chapter 6](../Chapter_6/Theory.qmd) we
combine them with the likelihood of this chapter to fit ecological response curves.

# Chapter quiz

The questions below follow the order of the chapter. Try each question before opening its
solution.

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 1: frog egg masses"}

You count the egg masses of a frog in eight ponds and write the likelihood
$L(\lambda\mid x_1,\ldots,x_8)$ of a Poisson model. Which quantities are fixed in this
function and which one varies? Does the likelihood give the probability that $\lambda$ has
a certain value?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The eight counts are fixed and $\lambda$ varies. The likelihood is the probability of the
observed counts for a given value of $\lambda$. It does not integrate to one over the
values of $\lambda$, and in the model $\lambda$ is a fixed quantity, so the likelihood is
not a probability distribution for $\lambda$. We use it to compare values of $\lambda$.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 2: mayfly nymphs"}

Two samples from a stream contain 2 and 0 mayfly nymphs. Assuming i.i.d. counts with a
Poisson distribution, write the likelihood as a function of $\lambda$ and evaluate it at
$\lambda=1$ and at $\lambda=2$. Which of the two values is better supported by the data?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The likelihood is

$$
L(\lambda\mid 2,0)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{2}}{2!}\times e^{-\lambda}
=\frac{e^{-2\lambda}\lambda^{2}}{2}.
$$

At $\lambda=1$ it is $e^{-2}/2\approx 0.068$ and at $\lambda=2$ it is
$4e^{-4}/2\approx 0.037$. The data are better supported by $\lambda=1$, which is the mean
of the two counts.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 3: bat passes"}

A detector records the number of bat passes on each of 300 nights. Why would you calculate
the log-likelihood of a model for these counts and not the likelihood? Write an R
expression for the log-likelihood of a Poisson model with a mean of 12 passes per night,
for counts stored in a vector called `passes`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The likelihood is a product of 300 probabilities, which can be smaller than the smallest
number that the computer can represent, so R may return zero. The log-likelihood is a sum
of log probabilities and does not have this problem:
`sum(dpois(x = passes, lambda = 12, log = TRUE))`.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 4: germinated seeds"}

You minimise an NLL for the mean number of germinated seeds per tray, in which the
parameter is the logarithm of the mean. `optim()` returns `par = 1.7`, `value = 96.4` and
`convergence = 0`. What is the estimate of the mean? What is the maximum log-likelihood?
What does the convergence code tell you?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The estimate of the mean is $e^{1.7}\approx 5.5$ germinated seeds per tray. `value` is the
minimum of the NLL, so the maximum log-likelihood is $-96.4$. A convergence code of zero
means that the algorithm stopped normally.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 5: empty nest boxes"}

Under a Poisson model, the MLE of the mean number of eggs per nest box is 2.3. What is the
MLE of the probability that a nest box has no eggs? Which property of maximum likelihood
did you use?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

Under a Poisson model the probability of a count of zero is $e^{-\lambda}$. By invariance,
its MLE is $e^{-2.3}\approx 0.10$.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 6: parasites on fish"}

For counts of parasites per fish under a Negative Binomial model, the method of moments
and maximum likelihood give the same estimate of the mean but different estimates of the
shape $k$. How can two methods give different estimates from the same sample? Which of the
two estimators is more precise in a large sample?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The two methods use different information. The method of moments chooses the parameters
that reproduce the mean and the variance of the sample, whereas maximum likelihood chooses
those under which all the observed counts are most probable. In a large sample the MLE is
the more precise of the two, because it is asymptotically efficient.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 7: two curves for one parameter"}

For the half-saturation parameter of a model with three parameters, the range of values
within 1.92 units of the maximum log-likelihood is 2.1 to 2.9 when the other two
parameters are fixed at their estimates, and 1.8 to 3.4 when they are re-estimated for
each value. Which of the two is a slice and which is a profile? Which would you report as
a confidence interval, and why is the other one narrower?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The first is a slice and the second a profile. The confidence interval is the one from the
profile, 1.8 to 3.4. The slice is narrower because it treats the other two parameters as
if they were known, whereas the profile takes into account that they are estimated from
the same data.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 8: two surveys"}

Two surveys estimate the same detection probability by maximum likelihood on the logit
scale. The Hessian of the NLL is 16 in the first survey and 64 in the second. Calculate the
standard error of the estimate on the logit scale in each survey. In which survey is the
log-likelihood more sharply curved, and what does that say about the data?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The standard errors are $1/\sqrt{16}=0.25$ and $1/\sqrt{64}=0.125$. The log-likelihood of
the second survey is more sharply curved: it contains four times as much information about
the parameter (for example, because it has four times as many observations), which halves
the standard error.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 9: seed predation"}

The relative profile log-likelihood of a seed predation rate is $-0.8$ at a rate of 0.10
per day and $-2.6$ at a rate of 0.20 per day. Which of these two values is inside the 95%
profile likelihood interval? Which cutoff would you use for a joint 95% confidence region
of two parameters?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

A rate of 0.10 per day is inside the interval, because its relative profile log-likelihood
is above $-1.92$, and a rate of 0.20 per day is outside. For a joint region of two
parameters the cutoff is half the 0.95 quantile of a chi-squared distribution with two
degrees of freedom, `qchisq(p = 0.95, df = 2) / 2`, which is approximately 3.00.

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-important title="Question 10: flower visits"}

A Poisson model fitted to counts of flower visits has a maximum log-likelihood of
$-412.6$, and a Negative Binomial model fitted to the same counts has $-389.2$. Calculate
the AIC of both models. Which model is preferred? Does this tell you that the preferred
model describes the counts well?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}

The Poisson model has one parameter, so $\mathrm{AIC}=2+825.2=827.2$. The Negative
Binomial model has two, so $\mathrm{AIC}=4+778.4=782.4$. The Negative Binomial model is
preferred, with an AIC that is 44.8 units lower. AIC only ranks the models that we
compare, so it does not tell us whether the better of the two describes the counts well.

:::
::::
